That this House condemn this arbitrary and totally unfair taxation and inflation-fuelling policy which will hurt all retail employees and all Canadian consumers.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Oral Questions
The minister's budget papers indicate that he intends to include in taxable income any discount received by a retail sales person on the purchase of goods from the retailer. This policy means that every retail sales person must now receive a higher salary, which will then be passed on to the consumer. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am sure that the hundreds of thousands of retail employees across the country, and particularly retired ones, will keep the minister's answer in mind the next time they go to the polls. speechtext: Madam Speaker, one of the principal causes of the slowdown in retail sales which we have suffered in the past few months has been the very high interest rate policy followed by the government. subsubtopic: NUMBER OF FAMILIES PAYING INCREASED MORTGAGE PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Public Works who is in charge of housing. The last thing the people of Canada want at this point is a committee looking into bank profits; they want an excess profits tax to be levied and the money used for housing.
On Friday the Minister of Finance once again showed that he did not take housing as a serious problem. This was followed on Saturday in Thunder Bay by a spokesman for the housing industry who appeared before the NDP task force on the economy, saying, "Somebody is pulling the wool over our eyes,'' referring to the statements of the minister and others. That same businessman noted that in Thunder Bay alone there were more than 60 homes up for sale, subject to power of sale. Although those families do appear in statistics, will the minister admit that there are thousands of other families in Canada who have to pay $200 or $300 or more in increased mortgage payments now, who do not show up in statistics nor do they get any benefit from the government's budget?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: NUMBER OF FAMILIES PAYING INCREASED MORTGAGE PAYMENTS

Madam Speaker, this morning I had the opportunity to discuss these very concerns with the minister of housing for the province of Ontario. He was responsive to the initiatives that were taken by the Minister of Finance in setting aside $350 million for the next two years through the budget which would, first of all, assist people faced with mortgage renewal problems who had difficulty after they had to put a fair amount of their income toward mortgage renewal. The officials and the minister of housing for this province felt that would be of assistance to
December 7, 1981

many families at this time, Thunder Bay being one of the cities affected.
On the second point of interest rates, there is no question that the reduction in interest rates over the last five to seven weeks has made it much easier for people to meet increased interest rates over and above those that pertained when they took out the mortgages they are now seeking to renew.

speechtext:

Second, he did not answer the question that, notwithstanding the slight drop in interest rates, in my judgment, and in the judgment of those with expertise, outside the House of Commons and the industry, we are still left with thousands of families who are suffering because they have to increase their monthly mortgage payments. Considering that the final bank profits are now in, and they are up $1.7 billion, will the minister take some reasonable action and speak to the Minister of Finance and request that we have fair taxes for the banks; and specifically considering the fact that if their profits were at the same level at which they were last year, we would have $700 million in additional revenue which we could use for housing, will he request the Minister of Finance to levy an excess profits tax to get that $700 million from the banks and put it into housing?

subsubtopic: COST OF MAILING MUNICIPAL PUBLIC UTILITY BILLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation. The minister will be aware that the corporation proposes to force municipalities to send their public utility bills via first class mail at the planned 30 cent rate. These are bills which, in the past, have been delivered either by their own employees or by organizations such as Boy Scouts or Girl Guides for 9 cents to 10 cents per unit. This represents a 200 per cent increase in the cost of delivering these bills.
Is the minister not aware of the tremendous cost burden that this will place on these municipalities at a time when all levels of government are reducing their assistance to municipalities?

December 7, 1981
Oral Questions
If he is aware, is he prepared to take some steps to correct this injustice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: COST OF MAILING MUNICIPAL PUBLIC UTILITY BILLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Canadian Post Office has always had exclusive responsibility for carrying the mails in Canada. When we considered the Canada Post Corporation Bill, this matter was discussed at length and all aspects were carefully examined. Examples such as the one just given by the hon. member were raised at the time and were discussed and dismissed. I should also like to remind the hon. member that this bill was passed unanimously by the House, all members present on both sides of this House approving the bill.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I could see a step being taken to force the municipalities to do so at the 17-cent level, which would not be such an immediate burden to them, but to enforce something which has not been enforced in the past and at the same time to increase the rate to 30 cents is something which is not acceptable and cannot be carried by these municipalities.
The proposal that large municipalities can pre-sort in excess of 5,000 bills and thus pay a reduced rate of 21 cents whereas small communities with less than 5,000 subscribers have to pay the full 30 cents, is somewhat puzzling. Surely they can sort 1,000 letters in small post offices as easily and as quickly as 5,000 in larger ones. Does the minister not feel that this is an act of further discrimination against small communities that do not have 5,000 subscribers, and will he take some steps to correct this?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I feel it is not a matter of cost but of principle as to whether or not carrying the mails is to be the exclusive privilege of the Canadian Post Office. And as soon as we make any exceptions to this rule, it is obvious that only profitable routes would be attractive to private businesses, so that in remote areas of Canada, mail services would have to be provided by the Canadian Post Office. Now, in order to guarantee and protect postal services in the smaller municipalities, we must keep our exclusive rights in cities where the volume is much larger, so that the Canadian Post Office may collect sufficient revenue in order to provide the same level of service in all parts of Canada.

I feel that this gives us a good indication of the extent to which this very important bill has been considered by Parliament, and that, as the member for Etobicoke Centre on the opposite side said so eloquently, it is extremely important to proceed with its adoption. The Committee on National Resources and Public Works tabled its
report in July. We started debate on the bill in July, and when the session resumed this fall, Bill C-48 was practically the only legislation for consideration before the House until the debate on the Constitution. In fact, we debated and voted on fifty-seven motions proposed by the government and the opposition, motions that had already been considered in committee.
Madam Speaker, granted, there is a time for consideration, reflection and study, but there is also a time for making decisions. Parliament is not exclusively engaged in contemplation. Furthermore, Parliament should not be prevented from deciding on the bills that are before it. There comes a time when decisions must be made. Parliament must decide on matters that are of primary importance to Canada. Bill C-48 is one of the main parts of the government's energy policy and the program for Canadianization of the oil industry in Canada. It must be obvious to everyone that we must decide now what is to happen in this respect. I should like to point out that the government has been extremely patient and has shown every consideration for the wishes expressed by the opposition, both at the committee stage and during consideration of the bill in the House. I hope the members of this House will agree to proceed without delay to pass the bill on third reading.

speechtext:
For a number of reasons we shall oppose the government's motion of closure. The problem in the House has to do with the way the members are not made aware of the program that the government intends to proceed with during the course of any one session.
There are some serious problems that go to the very root of the government's intention to use closure time after time. I suggested some months ago during a discussion similar to this that there were other ways to order the business and affairs of the House that would allow all of the members to be involved. I suggest again that that would be one of the more constructive approaches that we might take to avoid the need to use closure under Standing Order 75c on an occasion such as this.
We are asked to make a decision that enough has been said about a very important piece of legislation. It is not for me to decide, nor is it really for the government to decide, whether enough has been said, whether all that should be said has been said and every opportunity has been given to members so as to influence the course of affairs of the country in a constructive, sensitive and sensible way. While it may be possible for me from time to time to think that enough has been said on any one topic, I suggest that that does not necessarily mean that it is the considered judgment of the vast majority of the members of the House that that is true. There are times when topics are raised in the House that I frankly think, after the first speaker has spoken, that we have heard enough; but that does not mean that in truth that is the case.
I should like to suggest that once one starts to use closure- and I think this is where the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is quite correct-with each attempt, with each usage, it becomes easier. Therefore, the test of whether or not every opportunity has been afforded all members to express their genuine concern on behalf of the people they represent becomes a test that, in essence, is not really applied equally or fairly in every instance.
I should like to suggest to the government one thing they might consider to avoid this kind of confrontation arising time after time. I believe at the beginning of every session members of the government, such as the House leader and perhaps others within that group who manage the affairs of the government for the House, should get together with the representatives of the official opposition and the NDP. Then they should sit down at the beginning of the session and go over the program for the particular session that the government anticipates it would like to see proceeded with and completed. We might then together prioritize that program in order to have our input in what areas we believe will be very controversial and how those areas can be best handled both in terms of the time allocated in the House and the time allocated in committee to deal with such matters.

December 7, 1981
Time Allocation
This is not intended in any way to inhibit the government's right to proceed with other matters which from time to time arise. But it allows us to look in the over all at all matters to be considered by government, within reason, and then to make a determination as to which of those matters are likely to evoke the most debate, which of those matters are likely to create the greatest uproar, and which of these matters are likely to take the longest period of time. Then we could, together with the government, make an effort to establish an order which would allow the government to proceed with all its business. At the same time it would allow the opposition to review adequately in the House, in committee and if need be back in the House, as was the case with this particular piece of legislation, all ramifications of the legislation. If we are ever to get to that point, the need to use closure would be so infrequent that we would not likely see Standing Order 75c used at all for the balance of this Parliament.
I put to those who manage business for the government that it is not nearly good enough to manage business on the basis of one week to the next. One cannot expect people to deal adequately with the legislative program of the government unless they are aware of what it is. One cannot deal with legislation if one is given notice of the intent to have the matter debated in the House and referred on Thursday for the following Monday discussion. In dealing with such matters in the Ontario legislature during minority government, it has been my experience that we were well able to look at the government's over-all program, to come to grips with those matters which were of vital importance to the majority of members and to put them into an order which enabled us to establish a time-frame within which they could be dealt. To the best of my recollection, we never had to use closure during the five years that I was House leader of the official opposition and of the third party during the time of minority government in Ontario.
We will not support this motion because it is a further slide down the slippery slope. I do not want to go any farther down it. I think we have seen enough closure in the House. Now we want to see co-operation and orderly dealing with the business of the House. The only way it can be done is if the government takes the opposition into its confidence in terms of what it proposes to consider over the course of a session and together we establish a way in which those matters can be dealt with adequately by everyone and proceeded with through the House and committees to achieve the ultimate result of passage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us relates to Bill C-48 which the House has been considering for almost a year. During that period, the draft legislation has been subjected to most careful and detailed scrutiny which has surpassed that given to most legislation before the House. The complexity of the bill and the magnitude of the task that the legislation must accomplish requires no less than the careful scrutiny the bill received.
Over a six-month period, the bill was before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. At more than 70 meetings of that committee, hon. members heard testimony from officials and received deputations and representations from a variety of Canadians from the Arctic, from sub-Arctic areas and from the Atlantic and Pacific regions-in fact from all Canadians who have a real interest in the development of petroleum resources in the Canada lands. In all, 140 witnesses appeared before the committee to give their views on the bill. Some of their suggestions, when incorporated with those presented by hon. members of the opposition, assisted the government in putting forward some 100 amendments for the draft legislation. Since the adoption of the amendments, another 57 amendments have been brought forward in the House, most of which simply repeated suggestions put forward in committee. We have allowed every opportunity for a fair and full debate. Perhaps we have even been overly flexible with respect to the length of debate on Bill C-48. Indeed, there were some 235 major interventions on the bill during the course of consideration in the committee and in the House. The bill has, in fact, been before us for a period longer than the constitutional resolution. There comes a time when the House must make its decision. That time has now arrived. We on this side of the House assume responsibility for taking that decision.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) spoke against time allocation on Bill C-48, but he knows as well as I the reasons why such allocation has now become necessary. It is the obstruction on the part of hon. members of the opposition which has delayed the passage of this important legislation.

Clearly unanimous approval of every aspect of Bill C-48 was not to be expected, but there is no question that the legislation is long overdue. For years we have operated under anachronistic legislation which would have been improved at an earlier
December 7, 1981

stage by Bill C-20, but that bill died at a time when a general election was called.
I have no disagreement with the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) who, almost a year ago today, made the following statement:
The broad objectives of this legislation are worthwhile and certainly acceptable. One might go so far as to say that they are motherhood; they are intended to increase production and Canadian ownership, as well as to provide a very stable tax environment. I agree with that, Mr. Speaker. It is basically for this reason that we have brought forward a motion for time allocation at this stage. During the past year major agreements have been reached with the governments of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. At the moment we are engaged in serious discussion with the governments of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and British Columbia with regard to offshore resources.
An attractive price regime has now been established. That is one incentive for the more rapid development of the petroleum resources in the frontier lands which, when taken in conjunction with the petroleum incentive program, will ensure that Canada achieves oil self-sufficiency to match our self-sufficiency in other energy forms.
Against this background, I cannot understand how the official opposition can justify their continued obstruction of a bill which will ensure, among other things, greater Canadian participation in the Canada lands. For many years, we on this side and some members of the New Democratic Party have urged that legislation be put in place to ensure that Canadians have a greater opportunity to participate in the development of their own petroleum resources. This bill contributes to that objective, Mr. Speaker. When coupled with other aspects of the National Energy Program, it will ensure that, for the first time, Canadians have a real opportunity to participate in their own petroleum development.
That policy has the broad support of the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker. A recent survey conducted by the Canadian Petroleum Association showed that 84 per cent of the people surveyed support the thrust of the legislation now before us. Not only does the great majority of the public support such a policy, but so does the government of Alberta which has undertaken to offer petroleum incentives which, among other things, will enhance the Canadianization of our petroleum industry. So also does the government of Saskatchewan. So does the government of Ontario also for example, supports this Canadianization, as we have seen from its recent acquisition

Mr. Speaker, the hypocrisy of the parliamentary secretary never fails to amaze me. He can stand up and spout things that I know he does not believe. He can take the most outrageous misinterpretations of statements made by members of this party and put them forward as fact. I must say that he serves the right minister in terms of the fidelity with which he treats facts and presents them to the House.
The parliamentary secretary said that my colleague, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), had indicated that it is about time this bill came forward because we have been waiting ten years for it. I should like to set the record straight, Mr. Speaker. Ten years is approximately right; in fact, it is 11 years. In April, 1970, the then minister of energy in the Liberal government said that the government was withdrawing the rules and regulations for Canada lands in order to replace them soon with better rules and regulations. "Soon" was seven years! In 1977 the government brought forward a set of regulations which were not good, but were not bad. As a result of what they brought forward then there was a spurt of activity in the north. Then came the National Energy Program which brought to a halt much that was being accomplished and that we had expected would continue in the north.
The parliamentary secretary said that great progress had been made as a result of the National Energy Program. He pointed to the agreements made with the provinces as examples of progress. As a result of those agreements, however, the federal government abandoned its crude oil pricing schedule for domestic crude, it abandoned the export tax on natural gas and it abandoned the proposal to treat old oil and new oil in the same way. What he calls the great progress in the National Energy Program was really backtracking from some of the more absurd proposals that were brought in in the first place. That is what the government defines as progress, Mr. Speaker.
Judging from statements he made at the Liberal Party convention in Toronto a couple of weeks ago, I know that the parliamentary secretary will join with me in hoping that we see progress in the budget very soon because there is a need for more backtracking there as well.
The parliamentary secretary says that we should be pleased with the national energy policy and what it is achieving. I have before me the latest issue of Oilweek magazine which quotes the minister as saying, "I wish to refer hon. members to the figures published in Oilweek magazine". So the minister uses figures from this publication. A chart in the magazine shows that on November 18, 1981, there were 281 rigs drilling, while on November 18, 1980, there were 446 rigs drilling. Is that progress, Mr. Speaker? In one year half of the drilling capacity in the country has been wiped out. The parliamentary

December 7, 1981
Time Allocation
secretary seems to think that is progress. A little more progress like that and there will be no rigs drilling at all, Mr. Speaker. That will be just marvellous progress!
There is no question that this bill has been before us for a long time, Mr. Speaker, but we have not been dealing with it exclusively for a full year. I can recall taking a few months off last summer and talking about the Constitution and the budget. Other subjects were raised during the year that interfered with the debate on Bill C-48 as well.
It has taken so long to go through the House because it is a bad, bad bill. It is one of the worst bills ever brought forward by any government. It establishes a precedent for the democratic free world. I have researched this subject, Mr. Speaker, and it appears that this is the first time in any democracy that a government proposes to confiscate private property without compensation. It is the first time any democratic government in any democratic free nation has presented this kind of legislation. That is an incredible precedent, Mr. Speaker, and a year is not nearly long enough to discuss the bill fully.
Perhaps the parliamentary secretary should go over to the Senate and listen to the discussion on the bill there. He claims that everything that needs to be said has been said, but if he were following the proceedings before the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce he would realize that a lot more needs to be said.
Far from being perfect or even getting a passing grade, this bill is a bad piece of legislation. We would do Canada a service if we were to toss it out. If we were really interested in Canada and not in the political reputation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), that is what we would do. If we were dealing with something other than political pride, then hon. members opposite would join us in throwing this bill out, throwing it back to the bowels of the civil service where it came from, because it is an atrocious piece of legislation. I would certainly identify with the problems which were alluded to by the House leader for the New Democratic Party concerning the way this House functions, the necessity to co-operate, and so on.
It is frustrating in the extreme, to go before a committee, to debate in the House, to discuss in Committee of the Whole or whatever procedure, bills of such tremendous importance as this bill and, whether sitting around the committee table or in the House, be faced by a bunch of members who know that their only purpose and reason for being there is to say "aye" when the minister orders it. Independent thinking is intolerable to the backbenchers or frontbenchers of the Liberal Party. They do not tolerate independent thinking. Therefore, I can perhaps understand some of their frustration and the reason they applaud bringing in closure today. It is because they have been sitting there for a year, with different characters coming in and participating in different stages, but they have not been allowed to have a single independent thought, and they have not been allowed to examine the legislation from any other point of view. They must always say, "Is this not wonderful?
The minister is such a brilliant man! This Liberal government is so sensational!" Their sole role is to say, "Aye, sir, aye", when ordered to do so. They are never allowed to think. If they dare think, they will be back there behind the curtains forever. Their chances of going on a trip? Zip! Their chances of becoming parliamentary secretaries? Zip! Their chances of getting any of these nice perks are shot if they ever dare think. Therefore, "For goodness sakes, do not think!" is the cardinal rule of the Liberal backbencher. They must say, "Aye, aye, aye!"
If they were thinking, and I assume that some of them have the capacity of doing so from time to time, they would have listened to some of the things said. Yes, they might have heard some things being said by the industry, which many of them hate. However, they would have listened. Perhaps, if they did not like what the industry had to say, they would have listened to what the legislative council in the Northwest Territories and the legislative council of the Yukon Territories had to say. They would have heard their concerns. They would have heard their feelings of exasperation at being treated as a bunch of colonials by this bill.
What this bill does for the Northwest Territories and Yukon is the same thing that the Dutch East India Company did to India. The government established Petro-Canada as a kind of governor of this enormous territory. This benevolent Crown corporation will now have more to do with the development of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon than the democratically elected legislatures of those two territories. It is colonialism of the worst sort.
If hon. members opposite had the capability to think, they would have thought a little bit about what those people were saying. They would have thought about what those democratically elected legislators were saying. Hon. members would have said, "Maybe we should not be so rash in the manner in which we put forward this legislation".
This situation is really sad. I think that this House would do itself a service by devoting several days of debate and discussion to the quality of the democracy that exists and to the nature and way this place operates. The reality is that much of what we do is basically fraudulent. Hon. members opposite, and particularly backbenchers of the government party, sit in committee and participate in debate, claiming they are speaking as individual MPs. However, in fact they are automatons, robots who say, "Aye, sir, aye", and nothing more.
We call this a democratic Parliament, a parliamentary system which has its tradition; but in a sense we are deceiving the people of Canada if we claim that Parliament, in fact, functions as it should. It does not. Whatever comes out of the bowels of the bureaucracy, rubber-stamped by the cabinet, becomes holy writ.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, initially I did not intend to take part in the debate on the motion of closure presented by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), but considering that the debate on
December 7, 1981

the bill has been going on for more than a year, I feel it should be made clear to the members of the opposition that the line has to be drawn somewhere. Personally, I would be the first to protest any attempt to gag the House whenever a bill is at all controversial, if the time allotted to consider the bill was not sufficient. However, Bill C-48 was tabled in the House more than a year ago, and I feel that anyone who wants to extend the debate is clearly showing signs of bad faith.
Earlier, I was listening to the member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) speak to this bill, when he asked to extend the debate again for a few days, so that certain improvements could be made. The surprising thing is that during the ten minutes he spent talking, the hon. member made no new proposals aside from criticizing the measure of closure. In my view, if the hon. member had any desire to be effective, he would have used his ten minutes to suggest at least a few improvements, if he is so convinced there is room for any. One of the important elements that has been added to the bill during the past year, Mr. Speaker, concerns future discussions with native peoples because Bill C-48 is not placing any restrictions on the debate on land titles or rights that apply directly to native peoples throughout Canada. I believe that just now the member for York-Peel could usefully have proposed some concrete elements, in discussing native peoples and the environment.
In fact, Bill C-48 is intended to provide a framework for the implementation of new legislative provisions that are to govern the development of both gas and oil resources. This bill will help us exercise more government control over resources that belong to all Canadians. Of course this bill could be debated for ages. We could even add or delete a few commas! But let us at least give this bill a chance to be enacted. Later, if necessary, it could be tabled again in Parliament, when amendments could be proposed. Mr. Speaker, in debates like this one it is hard to understand why, instead of pressing on, instead of wanting to pass legislation, the opposition seems to be literally obstructing the parliamentary process and democracy. For one whole year, the opposition has had an opportunity to make its position clear, as have the members on the government side, and whatever the member for York-Peel may have said in this regard just now, he is very little concerned with the backbenchers of his own party or those on the government side. Members who were genuinely interested in the subject have all had an opportunity to speak to this bill, and to discuss it in committee.
So, anyone who says that we are blindly accepting measures presented directly by cabinet is ignoring the critical faculties of the members on all sides of this House. To the members opposite and to the members of my own party I can say that I have personally taken part in a number of discussions on native rights to ensure that the rights of these first owners of this country are not neglected by legislation that is of course creating a framework for the development of natural resources. The bill says clearly that in future, native peoples
Time Allocation
could claim any royalties to which they would be entitled. In no way does the bill affect native rights. It simply confirms the right of Parliament to continue to negotiate with the native people those provisions which could bring them revenue and also confirms their ownership of these lands for the years to come. It is important to note this. Another aspect of Bill C-48 which might be mentioned is the environmental aspect. In my opinion, some worthwhile provisions contained in this bill will guarantee the harmonious development of oil and gas resources and ensure that we shall have no cause to regret in the future whatever action is taken under this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to be guilty myself of what I deplore and talk about nothing, but I really want the opposition to understand, as we do on this side of the House, that some decision must be made after one year of debate on this issue. Something which many people deplore about the government is that we do not often have the courage to draw the line, even though imperfectly. Obviously, if I were to go over this bill, I might want to make some very personal changes and add my own personal touch to it. However, on the whole, I am satisfied. The bill provides guarantees which I am very happy to accept. We should at least give this bill a chance to see the light of day and quit dragging on about matters which have been debated according to the rules of democracy. In view of what was said in committee and all the representations made to the minister and to the standing committee of the House, no one can say that the process of democracy has not been respected.
I understand that some members may not be happy about this bill and that some people would have preferred another formula to ensure the development of Canadian oil and gas resources, but the fact is that the government is responsible for the decisions to be made in this regard. I believe that only the people may show their appreciation or disapproval of such a bill when they go to the polls every four years. It is important for the opposition to be heard and to express its views, but afterwards, we have to vote. As a last resort, the opposition will be able to revert to this issue in the next election, and if the people really condemn the government party at that time, they will obviously show it. Until then, the opposition should respect those that the majority of Canadians have elected to act on their behalf. This is important. We often have the impression that some people are trying to play a role or to speak on behalf of other people because they are convinced that only they can speak the truth.
Under a democratic system, the government is allowed to govern and the opposition to act in character, of course, and even to oppose measures, while abiding by the rules of the game, and making sure as well that no time is wasted. Considering the present economic problems in this country, I think it would be rather irresponsible for the opposition to ask for additional time in order to repeat over again same things that

have been said for quite some time in the House and in committee on that bill.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-48-MOTION MR. LALONDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand today with a sense of outrage. Today was the first time in over a year that I have put on my parliamentary button. I took it off the night after the brief debate when Liberal members opposite moved closure on the Constitution of Canada. Liberal members stood in this House and voted for closure after a short debate. This morning I decided that possibly the Parliament of Canada could work. I put on my button, and at my first opportunity to speak in this house I again face closure.
I would like to remind hon. members of the Liberal Party of Canada that they may have a tendency to blame the cabinet and the government, but their fund raisers, volunteers and votes in this House of Commons have sustained the government. Never in the history of this country have there been so many closure motions faced by a Parliament. Eight times members of this cabinet have moved closure in this House during this Parliament. I remind hon. members opposite that very shortly after the introduction of the constitutional resolution, closure was moved. A cabinet cannot do this. A cabinet cannot deny Canadians the freedom of speech which this House represents unless that cabinet is sustained by its backbenchers. I say to hon. members opposite that they must examine their consciences on each and every occasion a cabinet minister says that it is a good idea to move closure. Hon. members opposite must weigh the pros and cons to see whether or not they are culpable and part of a system which is gradually eroding democracy piece by piece in this country. Hon. members opposite must accept responsibility for that. I suggest to Liberal voters in Quebec, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland or wherever they are found that they must begin to judge members by the contributions they make to informed discussion and to democracy in this House.
It is our responsibility, and I will encourage our candidates in the ridings, to make voters aware of how often members opposite have stood in this House and voted for closure. There is nothing in terms of the long-term impact on the functioning of the Parliament of Canada that is as damaging as this record of closure.
The parliamentary secretary stood earlier in this House and talked about obstructionism. I put a different word on debate in this house. If we have a government that values this House,
then we should all learn from each other. We come from various parts of Canada. This is a forum. We come from Newfoundland, Vancouver Island and the Northwest Territories. We come to this chamber as representatives of people in our communities and regions. We come to bring that perspective to the debates of this House. The extent to which closure is used as a tool to cut off our instructional process is eroding public confidence in the ability of this chamber and the Parliament of Canada to act on behalf of the Canadian people.
On each occasion closure is used, it becomes easier to use it on the next occasion. The proof of that lies in the fact that we are considering the ninth motion of this kind brought forward by this government.
If hon. members opposite are pleased with last Wednesday's vote on the Constitution of Canada, I remind them that they could not have stood in this House and voted for that resolution or the accord if this party, led by the former prime minister of Canada, had not fought for seven days to keep them from getting to a closure motion. That is what the filibuster was all about; it was not on the Constitution of Canada. It was to stop the cabinet from moving a closure motion on the fundamental law of this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-48-MOTION MR. LALONDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand here today representing the people of Calgary West and facing a closure motion on Bill C-48, the Canada oil and gas act. There is a sense of tiredness in this party about trying to educate members opposite to the impact of this legislation on the future supply of oil and gas for Canadians. In my riding, in my neighbourhood and on my street, there are many people who work in the oil and gas industry as janitors, secretaries, engineers and geologists. I see them day after day. I have lived among them all of my life. I tell hon. members that the present bill will not produce the desired consequences. It will not produce the oil and gas Canadians could have and do need, the oil and gas which will become even more important in the future.
The minister has a choice. He can read the speeches of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) as a student trying to learn about the industry which is important to the future of this country, or he can read them with a closed mind believing that members on this side have no interests other than those of obstructionists.
In the meantime I say to the minister that a number of my friends and neighbours have left this country with their skills, their money and their equipment. They are not here today to help us find the oil and gas this country needs. One of the reasons they are not here is Bill C-48.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre said earlier today that never in the history of a democratic government has there been a piece of legislation which simply moves in, without compensation, to seal 25 per cent of the assets of people who have their money invested in the shares of these companies, includ-
December 7, 1981

ing the pension funds. What this legislation does is steal 25 per cent of the assets of Canadians who have invested in these companies, or in pension funds, without compensation. That is one of the things it does, and that is one of the things that has chased Canadians with talents, skills, equipment and money out of this country. The United States, Australia, New Zealand and other countries are benefiting from this policy promoted by the Liberal Party of Canada. This policy is probably more important in world economic terms than the North-South dialogue, particularly in its potential to influence events as we go down the road.
One of the problems results from his lack of understanding that in the world today, because of the actions of the OPEC cartel and things of that kind, there is a worldwide shortage of human beings with the skills, knowledge and experience needed to find oil and gas, get it out of the ground and into our homes, our cars and buses. These people are in short supply in the world today.
When the government decides to strengthen the hand of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and to trust the advice of its officials, then I suggest the first thing it should do is compare the salaries paid to the officials of that department with the salaries paid to those in the private sector. The minister should remember that there is a shortage and then ask himself whether in that competitive labour market he is getting advice from the best brains, the most knowledgeable people. Is the minister, who knew little about this industry when he started, getting the best advice? If the minister cannot come to the conclusion, on the basis of plain common sense, that the government can, is and will be competing in the competitive market for the best brains, then he better be careful about how much responsibility he is giving his officials and how much advice he is taking from them.
I suggest to the minister that any objective observer would have to come to the conclusion that a government department is never going to be able to get the kind of talented and experienced human beings required to run this industry. When the minister has that clear in his mind he should look again at Bill C-48 and recognize that for each individual play there is going to be a bureaucrat determining the rules.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-48-MOTION MR. LALONDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity of saying a few words on the motion before the House this afternoon to limit the time for debate on Bill C-48.
This bill is very important to all Canadians, and certainly to those involved in the oil and gas industry, with particular reference to the Canada lands, some 300 million acres in the north and on the east coast. The bill has been before the House for over a year now, and it is clear that even though it has had very extensive study in committee, with extensive debate at second reading and at the report stage, there is now under way a long filibuster on third reading.
Time Allocation
It seems to me that the opposition has the right to oppose a bill of this nature, but at some stage a decision has to be taken on what is the will of the House. During some 70 meetings the committee studying the details of this bill heard not only from representatives of oil companies but from people in the north and from other countries.
One feature of the bill that is often misunderstood, and about which there are outlandish cries of concern, is that feature regarding the federal government's 25 per cent share of oil and gas leases in the Canada lands. Bill C-48 does away with the existing system in almost all respects and adds one new element, namely, the 25 per cent Crown share.
Another related and very important component of the system is the federal government's cash incentives, the PIP grants, available to explorers, which will offset the 25 per cent Crown share. Thus there will be no free ride because the federal government is making grants for exploration. The government will be paying its way throughout the exploration and development stage and there will be no discrimination against foreign oil companies because they will receive the same 25 per cent cash incentive available to all Canadian companies. In fact, when the Crown agency converts to a working interest during the exploration stage, the federal government, in effect, will be paying nearly twice for its interest during the balance of that stage, because the private interest holder will continue to receive the minimum 25 per cent exploration grant in respect of his 75 per cent interest, while the Crown agency will pay 100 per cent of its working 25 per cent interest. Thus nearly 44 per cent of exploration costs will be met by or on behalf of the federal government.
Having regard to the fact that oil and gas resources are 100 per cent owned by Canadians in the first place, and the fact that Canadians have been funding frontier exploration and development through their tax dollars by an amount equal to much more than 25 per cent, Canadians should be entitled to at least a 25 per cent share of any oil and gas rights issued under the new act.
Regarding the 25 per cent Crown share of existing oil and gas rights, the rationale is equally sound. The fact is that Canadian taxpayers have been paying for the bulk of oil and gas exploration expenditures made in the frontier regions. Of the frontier development expenditures of $4.5 billion to $5 billion to date, some 75 per cent, or over $3 billion, has been provided through tax dollars in write-off provisions. Thus there is no case to be made for the suggestion that the 25 per cent Crown share is expropriation without compensation.
Furthermore, 85 per cent to 90 per cent of the total expenditure involved in exploring for oil and bringing a field into production is incurred after the production system has been approved. Since the Crown share will be in the form of a working interest not later than the time of the approval, the Crown agency will be paying a proportionate share of these major costs. That is, bringing the field into production and, as I said, paying 85 per cent to 90 per cent of the total expenditure. Of course, at that stage the Crown agency, whether it be Petro-Canada or another Crown corporation, will have con-

December 7, 1981
Time Allocation
verted their carrying interest into a working interest and will be paying their full share.
To ensure a fair distribution of past costs, there is a new provision for ex gratia payments on 25 per cent of the exploration expenditure made up to December 31, 1980 in respect of any oil and gas discovery which results from a well which is spudded prior to that date and which qualifies to be declared a significant discovery prior to December 31, 1982. The amount of payments to be made out of the Crown share of production will be fully reflected in the value in time of the qualifying expenditures. Thus, the government cannot accept the views of some companies that repayment should be in terms of the full market value of their reserves which have already been delivered.
Finally, our attention should be directed to the significant difference between the current Canada lands regime and the proposed Bill C-48 package. Currently, holders of exploration rights are required to return at least 50 per cent of their acreage to the Crown, which could involve up to 30 per cent of their discoveries, prior to obtaining production rights. Furthermore, the rights holder thereby loses a portion of the production area of the field. While some explorers have said that this imposes less of a burden than the proposals in Bill C-48, their actions contradict this view. In several cases they have opted for special renewal permits on their entire acreage, thus accepting the 25 per cent Petro-Canada back-in. They have done this in preference to moving directly to lease, yielding 50 per cent of their acreage but avoiding a Petro-Canada back-in. They are thereby recognizing a preference for the new system which allows them, among other things, to retain production rights in the entire area of an oil and gas field.
I would like to emphasize again the point that the people of Canada actually own 100 per cent of the Canada lands and the oil and gas which these regions contain. This amounts to approximately 300 million acres. Private companies may explore and develop these oil and gas resources but only on the full understanding that the federal government, as the landlord, can set a regime that is appropriate to the circumstances and in protection of the national interest. This is a basic principle which all governments must follow in managing their resources.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems important to me that we move on with this bill now. We have been without firm legislation for the past ten years, since the oil and gas land regulations have been in abeyance. This bill has been thoroughly aired, both in the House and in the committee. People who are interested are now concerned about the delay that is taking place at third reading, when amendments cannot be brought in anyway. I think it is important that we proceed now to pass this bill. The House has had an opportunity to discuss it in detail. I believe it is a waste of time to filibuster this bill at third reading. We should be putting in place a new oil and gas regulation regime for this important sector of our economy instead of wasting the time of the House. I would urge
members to get on with the job and pass this bill and bring its beneficial effects into being.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are several types of legislation that this House deals with. One type of legislation is that with which there is a considerable amount of agreement from all sides, such as housekeeping matters which have to be dealt with rather quickly and expeditiously. We on this side of the House have tried to be as co-operative as possible as far as these issues are concerned. We have heard this afternoon that rapid consent has been given to approximately 33 pieces of legislation during this session of Parliament. If that is contrasted to what happened in 1979, I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that during this session of Parliament it is evident that we have tried to be much more co-operative than the previous opposition.
Another type of legislation is that of a financial nature, such as the budget, with which we know there will not be agreement. The rules of the House, under the Standing Orders, provide a system of time allocation so that these matters can be reasonably and adequately debated before they come to a vote.
A third type of legislation is the type that is before us today, Bill C-48. This is a highly controversial piece of legislation which contains radical and new ideas that are not acceptable to the vast majority of Canadians. The traditional system which has developed over the decades in Canada for dealing with this type of legislation has been for the government to introduce the legislation, but rather than deal with it all at once, debate it over a period of time. There is a process of negotiation which is supposed to take place, and until this government was elected, this process by and large did go on. A majority government would get its way but the process would allow for consideration of other ideas and for the government to modify the proposals which it would have put forward. This process would prevent a radical change taking place virtually overnight.
I believe that this parliamentary process is a good one and should be inherent in the Constitution of Canada. We are now seeing this parliamentary process being abused and thrown away by the government. It does not care for the established principles of democracy and parliamentary procedure. Had the government brought forward legislation similar to Bill C-20, it would have been dealt with expeditiously. Bill C-20 was considered by the government, the opposition parties, by the industry and by people in the areas which would be affected, and there was a general consensus that Bill C-20 was the proper way to go. All that work went for nought and the government introduced Bill C-48, a bill with radical proposals; the concept of Canada lands and the continued colonialization and exploitation which the government wishes to see continue in the north, the idea that the minister can hand out gas and oil dispositions to anyone he wants. You do not get in line to come on a first come, first served basis or put in a bid at public tender; you just go to the back door of the minister's office and ask for a disposition at some particular area and ask, "What can I do for you?"
December 7, 1981

The notion of the oil and gas lease has grown up over many years in Canada. Companies would know what they were embarking upon when they signed an oil and gas lease in the north or in the provinces which issued these instruments. That will not be the case any longer under this legislation. The best that companies can do is to have something called a licence to produce. I do not know what kind of title that is. I am not surprised that property rights were not included in the new Constitution. What type of ownership is a licence to produce? It is practically meaningless. The idea is that whether you want it or not, you are going to have Petro-Canada in there as a 25 per cent or more partner. They are going to take that 25 per cent from you. It is confiscation, not, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) said, obstruction on the part of the opposition. It is obstruction of the parliamentary process by this government; that is what it is.
Unlike the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Kelly), who I am afraid is beyond hope and redemption, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources must have some spark of intelligence beneath that flint-like exterior. If he were to bring that little intelligence that he possesses to bear on this question, he would see what he has been party to. He must be able to see what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has been putting him up to.
This has been a shameful display of government arrogance. This is what the government intends to do. It came in with Bill C-48, it is going to take 25 per cent, confiscate it and do all the other things I mentioned. The government is not going to brook any opposition. It is going to do precisely and exactly what it had in mind in the first instance. It remains of that mind, not having listened to any of the arguments proposed by the opposition, other governments in Canada that have been involved or people in the oil and gas industry.
During the committee stage, this party proposed between 50 and 60 amendments. How many of those were accepted by the government? I will tell the House how many. Not one single amendment. I can believe that, out of the 58 amendments presented, after careful reflection 54 might not have been in the best interest of the country. However, I am sure that at least four, three, two or one, had they been looked at and carefully examined by members opposite, would have been found to have at least some merit. But no, that did not happen. The government made up its mind a year ago when this bill was introduced that it would not listen to the opposition.
That is one reason the government has run into so much trouble over the period of time it has taken. Another reason is all that has been going on in the meantime, all the time devoted to the Constitution and other issues. The government could have come in with Bill C-48, listened to the arguments and said, "No, we have listened to what you have to say and we realize that what you are saying makes some sense"-

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-48-MOTION MR. LALONDE
speechtext:
For Ottawa-Vanier, Mr. Speaker! I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words in this debate. I wish to remind the member who just took his seat that the House has spent twenty-eight days considering Bill C-48. There have been seventy committee meetings at which 140 witnesses were heard. I think it is time the government took action and that the House decided on this very important bill. Mr. Speaker, I also want to stress a very important aspect of Bill C-48, namely, the Canadianization of our industry. Bill C-48, an act to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, will enable the government to have more control over the development of regions under its jurisdiction, namely the Canada lands, and also to increase the level of Canadian participation.
This bill is therefore directly linked to one of the three primary objectives of the National Energy Program, Canadianization, which will give Canadians an opportunity to increase their participation in the energy sector, especially in the oil and gas industry. Mr. Speaker, one can hardly overestimate the importance of this bill, as it represents one of the major concerns of our National Energy Program. Its aim is to provide a basic framework for the sound management and profitable development of Canada's considerable oil resources, and more specifically in lands owned by the government in the North or adjacent to our coasts. The bill will also give Canadians a fair share in the development of their oil industry, while guaranteeing safeguards for the population and environment of these remote regions. Our program, Mr. Speaker, confirms the principle that Canadians are entitled to participate more fully in the activities of their oil industry, but it also wants to be fair to Canadians with respect to setting oil prices and royalties. These objectives are entirely compatible with our desire to guarantee the security of our oil supplies.
One cannot deny that Canadianization is progressing satisfactorily. In fact, the majority of Canadians are in favour of this measure. Since the National Energy Program was announced about a year ago, foreign participation has dropped by about 6 per cent and foreign control by about 10 per cent. Both the governments of oil producing provinces and the vast majority of Canadian citizens are supporting our Canadianization efforts. It is clear that Canadians see the National Energy Program and the Canadianization project as the two key stages in achieving two objectives, namely, 50 per cent Canadian participation and energy self-sufficiency by the end of this decade. If we take into account the rate of Canadianization since the National Energy Program was announced, we can safely assume that we are close to achieving these two objectives. Actually, the Canadian oil and gas industry can look to a

December 7, 1981
Time Allocation
very promising future, thanks to the National Energy Program and to these specific provisions of Bill C-48.
Naturally, as a state-owned corporation, Petro-Canada is committed to promoting Canadianization, and more specifically, the growth of our national industrial capability for providing the goods and services required for oil exploration. I want to stress the importance of the Canadianization program in connection with the development of our resources in offshore areas adjacent to the coasts. Thanks to this provision, Canadian industries will not only be taking part in the exploration of offshore resources, they will also be providing the equipment required to explore these resources. The National Energy Program also requires companies engaged in prospecting for oil and gas in offshore areas adjacent to the coasts and in the Canada lands to allow Canadians to compete on a normal basis as suppliers of goods and services. The Canadianization of the ancillary land facilities will allow new jobs to be created in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces and promote industrial development. Moreover, the use of Canadian goods and services will contribute to the development of new techniques likely to be exported which may have positive effects on our balance of payments.
Thanks to the Canadian corporation Petro-Canada and the oil incentive program, as well as the other measures which favour Canadianization under the National Energy Program, Canadians will participate to a large extent in the development of our offshore resources. Mr. Speaker, Petro-Canada is playing an increasingly important part in achieving the Canadianization objective set forth in the National Energy Program and the specific aims of Bill C-48. Over its past five years of operation, Petro-Canada has acquired much experience as an active participant in the Canada lands, a high degree of operational efficiency, and has played an active part in the development of new technologies, as well as an important though modest part on various international scenes. Since 1976, the corporation has been involved in digging 90 of the 153 wells in frontier areas and has been associated with the projects involved in every oil and gas discovery both on the east coast and in the Arctic islands. The corporation has for two years been operating drilling boats off the coast of Labrador, one of the most difficult drilling areas in the world, and it is now operating a drilling program off the Nova Scotia continental shelf. It is the only wholly-Canadian oil corporation in Canada, ranking sixth among the major oil and gas corporations, and it is involved in oil products marketing. I have had the pleasure to see Petro-Canada signs in my own constituency, and I feel that we should be proud to have Petro-Canada service stations in our constituencies.
Because of the experience it has gained, Petro-Canada has reached the following conclusions, and I should like to summarize these conclusions about the corporation and the impact Bill C-48 will have on the energy policy. Mr. Speaker, foreign investments in Canada's petroleum and gas industry are higher
than in any other country, a fact which is reflected in the number of permits held on Canada lands as much by the extent of foreign ownership as by the size of individual international oil companies' land holdings. If we are to make room for Canadians, Mr. Speaker, and if we do not want to wait for years and years before production begins in the less promising remote expanses of land, it is imperative that we make changes in the land system. The aims and techniques set forth in Bill C-48 are moderate under the circumstances, they are not unheard of on international oil markets, and they are geared to the purposes of the energy policy.
Mr. Speaker, the Canada lands are a huge area of sedimentary basins whose enormous potential requires large scale and high risk investments; skilful development and sophisticated technology are necessary. That region must have a competitive commercial environment and uninterrupted participation on the part of international corporations while we encourage new Canadian investments in frontier areas. The proposed tax system and land management meet that requirement. Just like any other country whose oil potential is significant, Canada must strike the proper balance between measures designed to encourage activities which generate new supplies and its desire to achieve a balanced and orderly industrial energy growth and responsible tax levies on the development of its new supplies. The policy appears to be commercially attractive and internationally competitive, and it will bring on stream the desirable contribution of the Canada lands so as to achieve self-sufficiency sooner than expected. Bill C-48 also sets up the structure for the deliberate action required if we want to offer full and competitive business opportunities to Canadian industrial, engineering and service companies. Those are my opinions, Mr. Speaker, after serious reflection, and they are shared by many members on this side of the House and, I believe, by many Canadians as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-48-MOTION MR. LALONDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is disappointing that we have to deal with Bill C-48 again by means of closure. Bill C-48 is one of the most important bills that the government has introduced in its short term and for the term it has had under its previous administration as a Liberal government.
In my opinion, the government has taken a very narrow approach to Bill C-48 in terms of what the bill attempts to do for energy production. So far as the future of Canada is concerned, it is certainly important. The bill also has a great impact on many people in Canada, not only those who are dependent upon producing oil and those who are consuming oil, but also on our northern people and on some important offshore resources that employ many Canadians.
I am particularly disappointed that the government reneged on a commitment in committee to put this bill and all its implications before the people in the north so as to allow them to have direct input. It is not sufficient with a bill of this
December 7, 1981

nature to expect the northern people, the fishermen on the east or west coast to compile adequate briefs on such short notice so as to make adequate representations of their concerns in Ottawa.
We are concerned that closure is being imposed upon us in the House without our having any legal information from the government, particularly from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), which would indicate what impact Bill C-48 will have on native land claims. We have been asking for that information for some time and it is not forthcoming. If anyone is obstructing the progress of Parliament, democracy and this bill, it is the government itself. The government certainly cannot expect the opposition parties to approve a bill that is so seriously flawed in many respects. Obviously, the "C" in Bill C-48 stands for closure.
The east and west coast fishing industry is poorly represented in Bill C-48, despite representations from the fishermen and allied workers in British Columbia, the Newfoundland fishermen, food and allied workers, the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee and the eastern federation of fishermen. We observe that little is contained in Bill C-48 that would indicate to those groups that the government is really concerned about protecting the offshore fishing resource which is so important, particularly in eastern Canada, the Atlantic provinces and Quebec.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) has been particularly silent on Bill C-48. We were expecting some comment from the minister. We were also expecting some comment from the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), who has so far failed to release the terms of reference as to how the environment will be protected under this Bill.
It seems to me and to the New Democratic Party that the only minister who has had very much input into Bill C-48 is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). In fact, it is a power grab not only for resources, but it is a power grab by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of the Environment. It is also a power grab to take away jurisdiction from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
We have just had an example in the Northwest Territories at Hall's Beach, where a cargo ship ran aground and we had pollution from diesel fuel leaking into that very sensitive environment. Bill C-48 does not address, in fact it confuses, jurisdiction over Arctic resources, Arctic pollution and offshore pollution in Canada. The Edgar Jordain lay on that beach for nine months before the federal government and its departments reached any conclusion as to how that particular oil spill would be cleared up. There were jurisdictional problems with the coastguard, the Ministry of Transport, the Department of the Environment, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. There also were jurisdictional problems between insurance companies and the ship owner. We cannot afford in our offshore and northern resources to have jurisdictional problems. The bill does not adequately address the
Time Allocation
jurisdiction and the responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and of the Minister of the Environment.
Also the bill is seriously flawed in the area of jobs for Canadians. My party has moved a number of amendments which would have provided some assurance that Canadians would receive the full benefit of this massive bill and its implications in terms of offshore, northern development and the types and number of jobs required if there is to be full scale exploitation of offshore oil and gas. Sourcing provisions have been ignored. Canadians should have the opportunities, particularly those in areas which are hard pressed by unemployment or dependent upon the fishing industry. We are looking to some alternative to fishing on the east coast. The people there should have had some guarantees in the bill. They should have been provided with an opportunity to build the necessary ships and oil rigs and to provide all the technology which goes into offshore exploration and exploitation of oil and gas. There are inadequate provisions in Bill C-48, despite the input of various groups such as the shipbuilding and mechanical industries, despite the amendments proposed by my party to guarantee that those jobs existed for Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in the concluding debate on Bill C-48. In particular, I want to use the few moments allotted to me this afternoon to read into the record of the House portions of the "Forum" column carried in the October 1981 issue of The Roughneck, a small spunky periodical which I believe is published monthly in Alberta.
I have chosen this column as my topic this afternoon for two reasons. First, it was written by a small producer who is a member of a group which, in the struggle between the Titans, is easily and often ignored. Second, its author, Joe Mercier, offered a rational-that is, a calm and balanced view of both the national energy policy and its critics. I should like to start with the latter, those critics whom hon. members of the official opposition champion so emotionally, vociferously and, as we have seen this afternoon, so blindly in the House. The author wrote:
-the National Energy Program is the long time work of well educated civil servants who feel that they are doing the best they can for Canadians. They won't be dissuaded by industry criticism that lumps them as inept, malicious facist-communists. Being avid readers of the industry press, they are quick to point out the inaccuracy, exaggeration and hypocisy of the industry arguments, especially those from the independents. Some examples they choose:
-Putting total blame on the national policy for the exodus of small Canadian producers to the United States
-Doing the same for the rig exodus and exaggerating the numbers -Pretending dismay and surprise at the 25 per cent back-in on Canadian lands when the industry was alerted to that provision in 1976 and provided with draft implementation of it in 1978
-Embellishing the opportunity in Australia without mentioning that the government back-in there will be 50 per cent, or failing to suggest that American targets are not as good as those in Alberta and are as subject to bureaucratic regulations and interference as are Canadian targets.
In dealing with the national energy policy, he critically pointed out:
No question-the small producer faces severe problems. He is overextended under high interest rates with little cash flow and no means of raising equity capital...
His largest, single problem is a lack of markets for natural gas ...
His second problem is the inability to raise equity capital. Stock prices are down and there is no assistance from government in improving them.
His third problem could well eclipse the other two-the unbelievable complexity and paper work, dozens of taxes, and production forms, drilling incentive applications and back-ins. Now we have to add proof of Canadian ownership rating applications and justification for PIP grants and proof of non-avoidance under the Canadianization rules ...
His fourth problem is a lack of input with governments chiefly because of the assumption by politicians that the larger independents are speaking for him.
For the small producer the recommended cures are relatively simple-for cash flow-bring rationality into the marketing of natural gas. If the bureaucrats in Ottawa and Edmonton and the large independents sincerely wish to help the small producer they should start here. Not only would a rational market save the small producer but it would at last bring an effective effort from the industry in making a creditable determination of surplus reserves, reasonable exports and expansion of the gas markets .. .
The largest contributions undoubtedly could be made by the federal government if it would allow a full tax write-off against other income for the purchase
of shares in Canadian companies. That provision alone would do more for Canadianization than any other provision intended for that purpose . ..
For a continuing input into government policies and regulations that affect us, we would suggest that the spokesmen for the... independents follow the example of the majors in making reasonable specific criticisms.
Obviously, Mr. Mercier is concerned, obviously he is anxious to defend and promote the interests of small producers and just as obviously, the small producers want to reach an accommodation with the national government that respects the basic interests and prosperity of both sides. I commend him and his point of view to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and to the members of this House.
