subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understand that I have roughly 15 minutes left in the speech which I started on November 18, 1981.
In my opening remarks I referred to the fact that, in the 13 years that I have been a member of the House, I never had the experience of seeing a budget which was so roundly and universally condemned. In short, I think that members of the House and Canadians at large are recognizing this budget as a formula for economic disaster. If one studies the budget, one can see that it inflicts irreparable damage and hardship on literally everyone and provides relief to no one. It provides no hope or encouragement and it is incumbent upon all of us in the House who believe in representative democracy to fight the passage of this budget in the hope that it will eventually be withdrawn. It destroys the motivation to invest, to produce, to build.
In the time I have remaining, Mr. Speaker, I will deal particularly with the dociiment entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the Eighties". All I can say is that it is a document which is couched in bureaucratic language that emanates from the ivory towers in Ottawa. It clearly offers

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski nothing in the way of hope or encouragement for increasing the productive capacity of Canada. In effect, it is really a job creation program for loyal Liberals because in that document one sees that there will be the creation of at least a half dozen commissions, task forces and boards which will serve to do nothing more than obstruct, frustrate and harass the private sector; all done in the name of outlining a new industrial strategy.
I must say that this is viewed in many quarters with some degree of suspicion. It is interesting to note the recent publication of a document entitled "Spectrum" put out by the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, the issue entitled "Canada's National Priorities and the Changing World Economy", written by Mr. Russell E. Harrison, chairman and chief executive officer of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. He points out that there are fewer than 20 years remaining in the twentieth century, the twentieth century that Sir Wilfrid Laurier said would belong to Canada. He further points out that we have but 19 years in this century to fulfil the Canadian dream to which Laurier gave expression-that our astonishing potential, our skills and our aspirations provide the basis for a strong economic finish to the year 2000.
He does point out that Canada ranks among the ten most important countries and economies of the more than 150 members of the United Nations. He also points out that despite our size and strength, Canada has lagged behind most other industrialized countries in recent years in the critical areas such as real growth, productivity gains, employment and ability to control inflation. He goes on to point out:
The dimensions of our national economic dilemma deserve careful scrutiny.
He points out that the four main aspects of our economic dilemma can be summarized as inflation, lack of growth, productivity and competitiveness. There is absolutely nothing in this document that addresses those crucial problems. He goes on to say:
Our problems are to a very real extent "made in Canada".
I certainly agree with that. He continues:
-we should be improving economic efficiency and encouraging new productive investment, especially in sophisticated high technology product and service areas ... The services sector is the most rapidly expanding sector.
We should be doing more to promote growth in the new high technology industry.
-our over-all investment in research and development, measured as a percentage of gross national product, ranks well behind other successful industrial countries such as Japan, West Germany and Sweden. ...
We can no longer rely on riding the coattails of a dominant world power as we have done for most of our history. There is no longer a single dominant economic power in the world, let alone one with which Canada has a privileged relationship. . . . An emphasis on one or two markets, especially ones which are our major competitors, will no longer suffice. We would do well to note that this is central to the strategy of successful countries such as West Germany and Japan. ... It is market forces-
He is referring back to this document which is supposed to outline a comprehensive industrial strategy. He points out that
you cannot rely strictly upon the guesswork of government to develop an over-all industrial framework. He points out:
It is market forces, not government guesswork, which should guide our economic development and our economic pruning. The industrial landscape in Canada and many other countries is littered with government-sponsored industrial concerns which challenge market forces rather than respond to them.
This is not to say that the role of government is not important, but the role of government does begin with the creation of a healthy economic climate that will contain inflation, provide for the responsible management of monetary aggregates, moderation in public expenditures and a stimulative taxation, regulatory environment, and an effective, longterm approach to energy pricing and supplies. It is this kind of structure and approach that is not contained in the budget and therefore does not provide any hope for our country.
It is very discouraging when one reads that document to find that there is nothing in it to give any hope to individual Canadians and companies to capture the tremendous wealth and potential that we have in this country. What else does the document say? It is almost laughable when one reads on. It points out that as an incentive to agriculture, this government announced it is going to have consultation to develop an agri-food strategy. It says it is continuing its review of the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
For the fishery sector, this government says it is reviewing fisheries policy. For forest-based industries, the government says it will continue consultations. For the mining industry, the government says it will continue consultations and make a report later this year.
For transportation in western Canada, the government says it will continue its meeting this year to try to develop an action plan. I should say there has been nothing done by this government to deal with transportation since 1979 when the Progressive Conservative Party was in office. All we hear about is the vanishing $4 billion western development fund which is now down to $1.3 billion. We are not sure what it is going to be spent on. Suffice it to say it is merely a slush fund.
The government says that to stimulate increased Canadian exports it will create an export trade development board to co-ordinate policy formation. In the final section of the Economic Development Paper on Human Resources, the government again skirts the problem in favour of inaction. It is going to review the labour market policies and have consultations to try to discover what initiatives might be taken for education and job training.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is trying to identify manpower needs and develop strategies to meet them. Canada Employment and Immigration is trying to increase its analytical capability. The entire strategy of this document entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the Eighties" reads as if the entire government had been on holiday for the last ten years and is now trying to engage in consultations and co-ordination, develop ideas, create new offices and agencies to try and figure out what is 'going on and then figure out what to do.
December 7, 1981

It will mean nothing more than an obstacle, another action of this government which will discourage investment and production and thereby discourage growth. This budget penalizes investment in this country. We need investment in order to create wealth, produce jobs and have individual Canadians exploit their full potential. We must have investment and increased productivity. We must have investment to advance technological change. We must curtail the mass exodus of capital, manpower, expertise and machinery which is fleeing from this country. There is nothing in this budget which addresses that problem.
As for the impact of the budget on the Toronto stock market, within a week after the budget was introduced it was recorded that the Toronto Stock Exchange index was reduced by some $6 billion. That is hardly an indicator of investor confidence. This lack of confidence comes on the heels of the 12 months of disaster that has been perpetrated on this country by the unfortunate National Energy Program which has been brought in. It has been disastrous.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Rubbish.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member says rubbish. He should go to western Canada and find out for himself. This National Energy Program is an unmitigated disaster. It has particularly hurt the drilling and servicing sector which is 95 per cent Canadian owned. With regard to the exploration sector, all that has happened is that this activity has shifted south of the border.
I had directed to me a copy of the October 5 Houston Business Journal. It is headlined "Canadian connection: Energy, money, politics blur borders". I quote briefly from the article:
Houston oilmen call the visiting Canadian oilmen "snowbacks". They began to migrate south in 1974 when the first signs of nationalism and anti-Americanism appeared in the rhetoric of Canadian politicians. But since October 1980, when the national energy policy was passed by Pierre Trudeau's government, what was once a trickle of snowbacks has turned into a deluge.
One unofficial estimate places the amount of Canadian exploration and development money spent in the United States since the passage of the NEP at about $2.5 billion. Much of that has found its way to Houston.
Several new oil and gas companies have been formed here backed by Canadian money. Large established Canadian oil companies, such as Dome Petroleum Ltd., have opened offices here. Many small and medium-sized Canadian independents have set up U.S. subsidiaries here to take farm-outs in U.S. operations.
They total something like two dozen new Canadian branch operations which have been opened in the United States. Some 226 rigs and more than 100 service rigs have left Canada for the United States. I quote:
Although designed for cold weather, many of the rigs have come to Texas. Some Canadian contractors are selling rigs to firms here rather than just moving them south-
In the Edmonton Journal of October 5 it is reported that some 235 rigs have now left Alberta for the United States as well as over 100 service rigs. Looking at that in terms of employment, each rig employs about 40 or 50 people and service rigs employ about ten people each. Imagine what that does. That is over 10,000 workers misplaced as a result of a
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
deliberate government policy. It is no wonder that division, anger and outrage is created in the country.
In my constituency of Vegreville The Wainwright Star Chronicle carried the headline "Jurassic quitting Canada". This is a very human story, Mr. Speaker. The November 25 edition of The Wainwright Star Chronicle reported as follows:
"It was the hardest thing I've ever had to do."
So says Jim Voll, who laid off 30 employees here and will take Wainwright-based Jurassic Well Servicing's remaining rigs south to Oklahoma.
The decision was taken in the light of federal and provincial policies which continue to destroy the small operator. . .. Last fall's National Energy Program . .. agreement in September set the stage for the move.
And the recent federal budget was the final straw. . ..
"There was just nothing in the budget to encourage us to stay."
Government induced depression in the oil industry here has meant there's just too little work here to remain in business. ...
The Wainwright-based company had operated 10 rigs from here, but sent six to the Oklahoma oilfields last spring. The final four will follow by the new year, Voll says, and the Wainwright office closed for good.
That is in my home riding; that is one of the major centres in my constituency. So much for Canadianization and the promotion of Canadian ownership! They are driving the expertise, the investment and jobs south of the border.
If one were to peruse the budget to see what it was supposed to do for Canadianization and promoting Canadian ownership, one notices that the taxes introduced in the National Energy Program, such as the petroleum, gas and revenue tax and the natural gas liquid tax, proportionately hit harder at the independent oil and gas producers, which are largely Canadian owned. It affects them more severely than the large multinational, integrated oil companies. There is nothing to redress that situation in this budget.
Second, Canadian oil and gas producers need now new equity and new capital to survive and grow. The November 12, 1981, budget restricts interest cost deductibility which will make this process more difficult.
Third, Americans continue to have full interest cost deductibility. Thus, foreigners will find it cheaper to invest in Canadian oil and gas activities than will Canadians.
Fourth, by deeming an interest benefit on loans made for employee stock purchase plans, it destroys a very important mechanism which many Canadian companies use to attract good staff and to motivate their staff to increase Canadian-owned shareholdings of their companies.
Fifth, the November 12 budget requiring the payment of taxes even for non-cash corporate reorganizations will severely affect the ability of many junior oil and gas companies, which are, again, largely Canadian owned, to reorganize their affairs so as to survive the adverse effects of other aspects of the National Energy Program. It penalizes those reorganizations and reduces the ability of junior Canadian oil and gas companies to contribute to the Canadianization of the oil and gas industry.

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
The National Energy Program is not a Canadianization policy; it is a nationalization policy. There is a fundamental difference between the two of them; there is no question about that.
Let us look at agriculture, a very important industry to western Canada, particularly to my constituency of Vegreville. As far as this budget concerns agriculture, it is a cop-out. Canada's farmers are caught in the squeeze of high interest, high inflation, high input costs and low commodity prices. In our society we know that farmers are price-takers. They do not have the luxury of passing on the impact of high input costs, high inflation and high interest to the consumer.

speechtext:
I want to thank my hon. friend for his courtesy; it is most appreciated. Maybe some day I will have the good fortune of returning that particular gesture. I do appreciate it very much.
I should like to deal briefly with two very important high input matters as they relate to the production of food. I think many farmers, particularly in eastern Canada, who have experienced a dramatic increase in the price of fuel, may very well be pointing the finger at the people of western Canada, particularly at the producing provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. It should be pointed out that at the present time Alberta and Saskatchewan sell oil for Canadian consumption at a figure of some $21.25 a barrel. More than $10 per barrel is tacked on in the way of federal taxes. This works out at a price of more than $31 at the refinery level. We are still importing some 400,000 barrels a day at roughly $42.38 a barrel.
The high energy cost, the high fuel cost, is attributable to the rip-off which is occurring by the federal government on the backs of the producers. Roughly 57 cents a gallon in the form of federal taxes is levied upon fuel which is used for the production of food. The excise tax of some seven cents is refunded upon application. So really 50 cents a gallon is levied against the producers of Canada for the production of food. This is a very substantial amount of revenue in the hands of the government.
As a matter of fact, if one were to look at the increase in the price of fuel in 1981, 75 per cent of the increase was attributable to federal taxes. Canadian food producers consume about
900 million gallons of diesel fuel and gasoline on an annual basis. If there is a 50 cent per gallon federal tax levied on that fuel, that amounts to some $450 million.
I believe it is terrible to think that the Government of Canada, which wants to pursue a cheap food policy, would have the audacity to impose that kind of taxation on the farmers of Canada who have no way of recovering that cost. Surely there is room for a 25, 30 or maybe even a 40 cents rebate. A 30 cents rebate would amount to some $270 million.
Let us look at fertilizers. At the present time the equivalent federal tax for the natural gas that is used for producing a tonne of ammonia is equal to $25 per tonne. Under the new energy agreement by 1985 the federal tax will increase to some $72 per tonne. If the federal government wanted to provide some relief to the producers of Canada, it could do so by modifying that tax. As it is, it is a federal government rip-off. There are substantial federal government revenues being generated on the backs of the producers who cannot recover and pass this cost along. The government is, in effect, penalizing the producers of Canada and not coming to their aid. I suggest that if this government were interested in preserving an effective food production system, this tax should be exempted or at least modified or reduced. It is one of our natural resources that should be used as a benefit for all Canadians, not as a benefit to or as an instrument for a major tax grab by the government.
We meet here today at a time when our agricultural industry is being severely threatened. It is a situation that is most serious throughout the country. Perhaps it is more serious in Ontario than it is anywhere else. Out of the 230 farm bankruptcies that have been reported since the beginning of the year, some 126 have occurred in the province of Ontario.
