speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address the House on the recent budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I must say at the outset that this budget confirms very clearly the government's firm commitment to economic leadership, the determination to counter the forces of inflation and to maximize economic opportunities for Canadians in all parts of Canada. This can be seen throughout the document. That is why I am strongly supportive of the measures which the Minister of Finance proposed.
The minister presented a responsible budget. Its themes of restraint, equity and economic renewal are certainly appropriate to the changing social and economic conditions we face in

Canada today. One of the ways the minister has striven to meet these goals is through reform of the tax incentive structure. A year ago he announced that he would take a hard look at tax incentives. He has done precisely that. Tax incentives tend to pyramid, with the result that a number of profitable corporations or wealthy individuals have very little or no tax. On the other hand, there has been a large group of individuals and corporations which have not been able to take full advantage of these tax benefits. These people and companies can be found primarily in the smaller communities of the country, in particular in those provinces which suffer most from economic and social disparities. That is why I welcome the review and that is why I applaud the results. Moreover, I hope the Minister of Finance will continue to examine and improve the federal tax structure, for I believe corporate tax incentives can be a very positive force for both national and regional economic development. The Government of Canada demonstrated that concern last year through the creation of the 50 per cent investment tax credit program which is helping to bring much needed development to those parts of Canada where it is sorely needed. I believe that further consideration of the regional effects of all elements of corporate tax incentives could contribute substantially to the equitable distribution of economic opportunity and to the more effective use of underutilized resources.
I am sure hon. members on both sides of the House recognize that national economic renewal cannot be achieved overnight; there is no quick solution. However, the budget and its accompanying economic development statement form the nucleus of a comprehensive economic approach to economic development in Canada which, if followed, will bring about the renewal we are all seeking.
This summer the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) was a member of the ministerial committee which prepared the new economic development policy framework. I know that the document entitled, "Economic Development for Canada in the Eighties" fully reflects his determination to deal with the problems of inflation, high interest rates and unemployment through a long-term comprehensive program of industrial renewal.
Today I should like to focus on the basic principles which will guide the direction of these national policies and programs, and to say a few words on what they mean for Canada's regions. Quite simply, the government's priority is national economic renewal. Its policy focuses squarely on industrial innovation, as well as the restructuring and improving of the processes of adjustment in all areas of Canada. To this end it states clearly that "regional economic development will be central to public policy planning at the federal level". I am most reassured by this statement, for I have long held that the regional character of Canada's economic environment is of prime importance to all of us.
Along with the Minister of DREE I have also emphasized the need for a comprehensive framework for economic de-
The Budget-Mr. MacLellan
velopment which must surely be based on the support and strengthening of our regional economies. I am sure all members of the House, and particularly those who were members of the Standing Committee on Regional Development who have worked closely with the minister, appreciate the complexities of integrating national and regional development objectives. The committee members in particular will also recognize that the main directions for the regional policy were enunciated in documents tabled at the standing committee some time ago.
The main elements outlined at that time, as hon. members will recall, were the development of human resources, the need to overcome barriers to growth, the requirement to promote industrial renewal and adjustment and to enhance interregional linkages by allowing the free flow of goods, services, capital and people within Canada.
Not only are these goals appropriate for the regional needs of our country, I am pleased to say they have also been given and accepted as central to the government's over-all policies and priorities for national economic development. It is now clear that this government is firmly committed to the development of our regions. This fundamental commitment will now be seen as being integral to the decision-making process of all our economic departments.
1 am most pleased with the central position that regional economic development has been given. DREE has fully participated in the formation of the government's new economic policy framework, and is now embarked on an elaboration of that statement for each region of this country that will enable this policy to become a reality.
The objective, if I may paraphrase the words of Ontario's minister of industry, is to forge and strengthen the economic links which bind our nation together. We must recognize that the Government of Canada cannot achieve these goals alone. Both the federal and provincial governments have economic development responsibilities. Therefore, joint planning and co-ordination is essential.
The federal government has forged some important new links in the past few months, first with the signing of federal-provincial agreements on energy and second with the federal-provincial agreement on a made-in-Canada Constitution, which contains a commitment by both levels of government to regional development and equalization. Let us continue to strengthen those links.
I believe that federal and provincial governments can and must work side by side to realize the economic opportunities that are before us. I also believe that the federal government's role in the implementation of regional development programs needs to be more clearly defined, recognizing once again that both levels of government have economic development responsibilities. Let us sit down together and discuss our plans and strategies. Let us seek to establish common objectives and priorities for regional development programs. Let us determine where the federal government can make its best contribution, and where the provincial governments can make their best contribution.

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. MacLellan
Planning and co-ordination of regional policies will be no less difficult than the energy negotiations or the constitutional negotiations. But I believe they can be equally rewarding.
A new set of economic relationships will build on our strengths which can be found all across our country. A new set of relationships will include the Atlantic region, Quebec, Ontario and the west in a genuine and just economic partnership. Co-ordinated strategies for the development of Canada's regions-complementary strategies-are essential to the building of that economic partnership.
The development of industry, natural resources, transportation, exports and Canada's human resources requires that the national government gain a thorough understanding of the circumstances and concerns in each region. Furthermore, the economic development framework accompanying this budget promises that special attention will be given to those areas of the country with the lowest per capita incomes and highest unemployment.
In this way, we will be working to reduce those economic and social disparities that exist between the various regions of Canada. These disparities are particularly prevalent in Canada's rural and more remote areas and among our native peoples. But in order to attack disparities, we must have accurate information for planning our programs. However, to date, even measuring these disparities has been a real challenge. But as members of the Standing Committee on Regional Development know, DREE has placed a high priority on the development of a small-area data system which will greatly assist our planning. It will also enable members of the House to gain a better understanding of economic circumstances in their own areas. In the near future, the Minister of DREE expects to be in a position to advise members of the House of a new, more comprehensive data system that will be able to respond to their real needs for information and statistics about their constituencies.
I would now like, Mr. Speaker, to look at some of the regional development issues we will face in the coming decade. We are indeed fortunate that throughout the 1980s, there will be genuine prospects for growth in every region of Canada. Of course, our regional dynamics mean that there are distinct problems that must be faced. The opportunities, as well as the constraints, must be addressed if we are to meet the challenge successfully.
The Atlantic region has areas that have begun to prosper in recent years, but there are also too many areas, such has my own constituency of Cape Breton-The Sydneys, where a great deal remains to be done. Nevertheless, the Atlantic region is, in fact, entering the 1980s well positioned for a decade of solid growth. The challenge here is to promote the expansion of enterprises capable of taking advantage of new markets, products and technologies which are emerging in world industrial markets.

Quebec is facing specific problems of industrial readjustment, especially in labour-intensive, low technology industries
such as the textile, clothing and shoe industry. That province has a large number of mature industries that will have to meet stiffer and stiffer international competition. While in the seventies emphasis has been put mainly on public investments, ways must now be found at all costs to increase investments in the private sector. Emphasis must be put mainly on high technology industries, promoting industrial research and the creation of export industries, especially those connected with the processing of national resources. Local and community development, aimed in the first place at areas where unemployment is highest and per capita disposable income is the lowest, must be a priority. We must also give back to Montreal its role as Canada's first trading centre, promoting the growth of its industrial and service industries and reconfirming its international status.
Ontario remains one of the strongest provinces in confederation, but there has been a relative weakening of its position within the national economy over the last decade. It is increasingly apparent that the Ontario economy must undergo a process of industrial renewal in order to adapt to changing conditions in international trade and to capture the opportunities which will be generated by major energy and other resource projects elsewhere in the country.
For several years, now, the west has been the fastest growing region in Canada, and the prospects for the future are that this rapid growth will continue. Economic growth has not been even, however. The west is now faced with a number of constraints: soil and water supply problems in the dry southern prairies; the inadequacy of the transportation systems, especially the bulk handling export delivery system; and, most critically, the short supply of skilled manpower. These, then, are the major regional development challenges we must face in the eighties.
I know that with this new policy framework, we will be able to meet these challenges. By recognizing the regional dynamics that underlie our country's economic and political structure, we will be able to achieve the renewal we seek, for economic renewal through the promotion of initiatives in the priority areas of industry, natural resources, transportation, exports and human resources can come about only through a development policy based on the needs of Canada as a whole, and its distinctive regional components.
As the government of Canada strengthens its capacity to integrate regional development concerns into its total policymaking process, I know that we will be able to make great strides toward achieving our goals of equity and economic renewal. This understanding of the needs of all Canadians in all regions is central to the economic development policies of the Government of Canada.
In this budget, the Government of Canada has pledged itself to the principles of equity, restraint and economic renewal. I,

along with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, endorse these principles.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I had as much enthusiasm as the hon. member who spoke previously with respect to the budget, because I listened with interest on November 12 last, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) presented his budget in the House. He stated that there were three themes to his budget: restraint, equity and economic renewal. With respect to restraint, he said, in part:
There is need for restraint on the part of the government and restraint on the part of all Canadians.
With interest rates running at 20 per cent, unemployment at record highs, more lay-offs on a daily basis, inflation rate at about 12.8 per cent, and increased energy costs amounting to an additional $1,400 a year per family, individual Canadians have little choice but to exercise restraint. The government's restraint program, on the other hand, is to increase expenditures by some 20 per cent.
The minister talked of equity and about an overhaul of the tax plan to clear what he called loopholes. It was a Liberal government and a succession of Liberal finance ministers who brought in these so called loopholes. But they were not loopholes when Benson, Turner, Macdonald and Chretien introduced them in the House. At that time they were tax incentives, incentives to encourage growth in the economy, to create new jobs, and to encourage construction and incentives for individuals to invest and for business to expand.
The Minister of Finance was a member of that government when all these measures were brought in. I do not ever recall the Minister of Finance, before he assumed his portfolio, standing up in his place in the House and saying that the measures, when they were introduced by former finance ministers, were unfair. On the contrary, he applauded them. On Thursday evening, November 12, very piously, in an attempt to cleanse his soul, I would suggest, he almost made it appear that those who had been making use of the incentives that he and his colleagues had passed as the law of the land were doing things which were not quite legitimate. I think he will have difficulty in persuading young working people who were borrowing money from the banks to buy RRSPs and claiming back interest as an expense, that they were taking advantage of a loophole; or that individuals who were making use of income-averaging certificates or who were deferring the capital gains tax after having sold the capital assets under agreements for sale were taking advantage of a loophole.
The minister spoke of economic renewal when he said:
This decade offers exceptional opportunities for strengthening and diversifying growth in every region in Canada.
He tabled a major policy document on economic development for Canada in the eighties, and the hon. member who spoke previously referred to that document.
In the last decade that I have been here in Parliament successive Liberal governments and finance ministers in the
The Budget-Mr. Neil
past have always talked of major policy changes, industrial strategy, and the opportunity for Canada and Canadians in the decade of the seventies. Did it take place? Let us examine the record. In 1970-71, the budget was for $14.6 billion. The last budget we have, the 1980-81 budget, is for $65.5 billion. In 1970-71, the beginning of this decade, the gross public debt was about $37.5 billion. In 1980-81, the gross public debt is over $122 billion. The interest on our public debt now exceeds our total budgetary expenditure of ten years ago. Our inflation rate has climbed to over 12 per cent. Unemployment is over 8 per cent, with almost one million unemployed people in our country. Bankruptcies of small businesses and farms are increasing, there are daily lay-offs in industries, and there are mortgage foreclosures because individuals cannot renew their mortgages and meet the high payments required monthly. Our standard of living is well below that of most developed countries.
We had exceptional opportunities in the seventies, and the government blew it because, under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Liberal Party has moved to the left, toward socialism. The government abandoned the principles of its predecessors who realized that this country was built on individual initiative and a free enterprise system tempered with compassion for the sick, the unfortunate and the elderly. The policies and the programs of this government has been such since the present Prime Minister took over that, generally speaking, Canadians have lost the initiative and the desire to risk their future and their capital on an enterprise which not only has to struggle in the marketplace, but, worst of all, is also plagued with complicated and uncertain tax laws, and, on top of that, government red tape, bureaucratic indifference and all the frustrations that go with the operating of a business.
It is a sad commentary on this great country of ours. The budget that was handed down on November 12 is of great concern not only to my constituency but to the whole of the country. Not only does it affect the economy, but it affects individuals and businesses.
I would now like to examine a few of the proposed changes. Let us consider the effect of the provision regarding interest deductibility. What does that mean to small businesses and to small corporations, and what will it mean to employee-sharing programs? I would suggest it means a drying up of capital and the possible disappearance of many small businesses. Small businesses are the backbone of our economy because they are Canada's major employer. Small businesses create jobs. Do we want to see business initiative disappear even further? Do we want to deny our young people the right to invest without a reasonable prospect of a return on that investment? More and more young people are reluctant to take over their parents businesses because of tax problems and government red tape, both provincial and federal.
Over the last two or three years I have talked in particular with two businessmen from my constituency who had excel-

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Neil
lent, well organized and well paying businesses. They had sons who, they thought, would take over their businesses. The opportunity was there for their sons. However, in both instances the sons told their fathers that in no way could they take over the businesses. With all of the risk, all of the problems and all of the government red tape, as well as the bureaucratic procedures that have to be followed, the sons told their fathers they would sooner get jobs elsewhere.
The sons went off to university, got degrees, moved out of the province and are working for major companies. There is a good chance those two businesses will disappear because the young people who have the initiative to make a go of business are not there.
What about interest deductibility that is being denied or restricted to the amount of income from investment? I ask the Minister of Finance what is the situation with respect to a young farmer who borrows money from the bank or the Farm Credit Corporation to buy some land? Generally speaking, because he has payments on machinery and other expenses, he does not really have an income. Is he going to be denied the right to claim the income that he pays on his loan as an expense? The government is not in a position to answer that question. The question has been asked. But that situation is all up in the air.
What about taxation on life insurance? Nearly everyone has life insurance. When one is young, newly married and starting out in life, one buys life insurance to guarantee that one's wife and children will be taken care of if something happens to the breadwinner. It is a secondary consideration that the insurance will create some sort of an estate for the individual on retirement. But what does this budget do? It taxes policyholders every three years on accrued interest and benefits. A few days ago I received a letter from Life Underwriters Association of Canada. The letter gives an example of a purchaser aged 25 who opted for a $25,000 whole life contract with an annual premium of $237.25 paid with after-tax dollars. By choosing to use his dividends to purchase paid up additions, he hoped to offset the ravages of inflation.
I should point out that the death benefit by the time this individual reaches the age of 73 totals $131,575. But under the present regulations proposed in this budget, this individual would have to pay a total of $28,357.43 in income tax on money that he never even saw. He would be paying that $28,357 out of after-tax dollars.
It is almost unbelievable what has been set down in this budget. There are proposed changes in the Small Business Development Bond program, but one has to be almost in bankruptcy before one can qualify for these bonds. I talked to a banker a few days ago and asked whether he was lending any money under the Small Business Development Bond program. He told me that he had been doing so for some time, but that since the budget came down he had not. "Why would I lend money to an individual on the verge of bankruptcy?", he asked me. "There is no government guarantee on the loan. I would be foolish to lend money," he said.
Let me refer to The Globe and Mail issue for Saturday, December 5, 1981. In it, there is an article about Small Business Development Bonds and the Farm Credit Corporation. Hon. members will recall that in the budget some $45 million was set aside to help farmers in need under the Farm Credit Corporation. I want to put on the record part of the article that appeared in last Saturday's The Globe and Mail. It commences:
Despite a flood of applications for the low-interest emergency farm aid promised in the federal budget a month ago, only three farmers across the country have received any money from the program.
The article continues:
Farmers can't apply for the federal money unless they have been turned down for a Small Business Development Bond first, and many banks have not been processing those applications because the federal government has not made clear who is eligible for the bonds, which the budget made available to unincorporated farmers.
On November 12, almost a month ago, the government handed down a budget. But the government does not know who qualifies for the Small Business Development Bonds. It cannot even tell the banks who qualifies. This is unbelievable.
Capital cost allowances have been cut in half for the first year. Has the government considered the effect this has on business, on industry and on farmers? Can the minister not see that this will have a very serious effect on the farm implement manufacturing industry and, on the farm implement dealers around the country? If farmers are restricted by the capital cost allowance, they can claim in the first year, they, along with other businessmen will not buy in the early part of the year. They will wait until the last day of the year. They would be foolish to do otherwise.
What concerns me, however, are the changes with respect to capital gains, particulary as they affect farmers and small business people. Over the years farmers and small business people have traditionally looked upon their business or their farm as the means by which they might have some money when they reach retirement to buy themselves a home and to supplement their old-age security pension. In many cases the only asset that a farmer and a small businessman has when reaching the age of retirement is land, inventory and machinery. When there was no capital gains tax in effect, there was no problem. In 1972 when the capital gains tax was brought into being as a result of the white paper on taxation, the problems began. Even so, a farmer or businessman had the opportunity of purchasing income-averaging certificates and the right to sell land or assets on time and to defer capital gains.
The capital gains tax has had a real effect on land values, and farmers are now faced with substantial capital gains. A farmer who sells his farm usually moves into the city or town and often buys a house, and it takes a pretty good chunk of the money realized on the sale of the farm to pay for that home. What does this budget do? It takes away the right of the person who has a capital gain to invest in income-averaging certificates. It takes away the right of a farmer or a business-
December 7, 1981

man to sell land or assets on terms over a period of time and to defer that income.
What is even worse is the fact that this government is changing the rules in the middle of the taxation year. This is just like running a horse race with the opportunity of deciding when the race is going to end. Obviously you will end the race when your horse is ahead. That is what the government is trying to do by changing the rules in the middle of the taxation year.
There are many farmers and businessmen in this country who, based on the rules, regulations and the law which existed this year, sold their farms and their businesses, anticipating they would be able to purchase income-averaging certificates until the end of March of next year. This opportunity was cut off on November 12.
I talked with one farmer who, as a result of the November 12 budget, will be faced with a tax liability of some $100,000.
1 talked to another farmer who wanted to make arrangements to divide his land among his family to be disposed of on his death. As a result of this budget, he is faced with a tax liability of some $71,000 and he has only three quarters of a section. This is unbelievable.
It seems to me that the very least this government could do is to say to those farmers, businessmen and people who incur a capital gain this year and who have based their sales and plans on the laws that existed, the law will not be changed as of November 12 but will remain the same until the end of the taxation year. That is only fair. In a few minutes I will come to another aspect of the unfairness of this budget.
Having regard to capital gains, I suggest that the minister should set up an all-party committee to consider perhaps the elimination of the capital gains tax, the exemption of capital gains from taxation up to a certain amount, or perhaps the updating of the valuation day. This was promised by the Liberals in the 1979-80 election campaign. The present leader of the Liberal Party in Saskatchewan said at a news conference in Regina, "If you elect a Liberal government, we will update evaluation day." What did the Liberal government do? It took away any benefit the farmer or businessman had when it comes to capital gains.
Such a committee should also give some consideration to the Farm Credit Corporation. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has complained about money being expensive. The interest rates on loans from the Farm Credit Corporation have increased I believe to 16.25 per cent or 16.75 per cent.
On numerous occasions members of this party, including myself, have suggested to the minister that perhaps one solution to the capital gains situation in relation to farmland would be to allow farmers who have capital gains to invest the capital gain portion of the selling price with the Farm Credit Corporation in the form of bonds. If a farmer did this and undertook to leave the money there for a period of five years, there would be no capital gains tax on that portion. The farmer could be paid interest at the rate of 5 per cent or 6 per cent, and that would not be taxable. The result would be that money would be made
The Budget-Mr. Lang
available to farmers at cheap rates, particularly to young farmers.
I should like to read part of a letter I received the other day from a young farmer. He says:
I am ... 21 years old and have lived on the farm all of my life. I now wish to farm for a living and am now renting three quarters of (a section of) land. I now have an opportunity to buy a half section of land. My father is well established financially and operationally but he is a small farmer and is limited in helping me get established. He is helping by renting his machinery to me and is partly financing me to buy this land. I will be working it off in a construction job and will subsidize my farming operation with this income.
Although all these things are in my favour (my young age, experience of living on the farm and renting land, my father's help with machinery and financing me, my subsidizing the farm) I find that a loan from Farm Credit Corporation at its high interest rate makes repayment possibilities so close and risky it is unsafe and unwise to buy.
He wrote to me and asked, "What can I do?"
1 would suggest to the Minister of Finance that he examine the proposal put forth by this party to allow farmers to put capital gains into the Farm Credit Corporation which would enable it to lend money to young farmers at perhaps 7 per cent or 8 per cent, a rate with which they could live.
Finally I come to the matter of taxation of severance pay. The taxation of severance pay rules apply to all public servants, members of the armed forces and the RCMP or anyone who receives superannuation from the government. Within the last week I have had two telephone calls from people who are government employees, one in the Armed Forces and the other in the RCMP. They face compulsory retirement because of their age. They knew what the tax law was, and they made their arrangements based on that law. The money that they were expecting to put into RRSPs or income-averaging securities never came in time to beat the November 12 budget. What happened is that these individuals are now faced with the fact that their severance pay is completely taxable. One of these people is faced with a tax burden of $7,000 or $8,000. It is absolutely unfair that the rules were changed in midstream. The Minister of Finance and the bureaucrats who worked on this budget never considered the effect of this budget on individual Canadians, the farmers, businessmen and corporations. If they had, they would not have brought in a budget such as this.
It is clear that the budget has caused hardship, confusion and anger across the country. One solution would be for the government to withdraw this budget, but I doubt very much that it would do so.
I suggest that the provisions of this budget should not be implemented until they can be studied by the various concerned committees. If the Minister of Finance is not prepared to do this, I think his only alternative is to resign.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I will take three approaches; the economy in general, the budget in relation to the economy, and then the international influence on our economy.

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Lang
The number one complaint about the economy that I hear from my constituents in Kitchener is not inflation. It is, rather, a combination of feelings and thoughts which I would characterize as uncertainty, fear, anger and hopelessness. This mood of the people is a number one problem. They do not have any confidence or belief that our economic problems can be beaten and, without that confidence, there is less chance that any measure directed at dealing with the economic problems facing us will be accepted as a positive course or that it will have a positive impact.
The Minister of Finance emphasized that point and its importance in his budget speech when he said, "The key which can open the door to our future is a change in our attitudes and expectations. We will move much more quickly to noninflationary growth if the conviction spreads that we are heading back toward stable prices and lower interest rates".
People do not expect miracles. Canadians have tightened their belts, but they do not want to tighten their belts on a rollercoaster that is leading nowhere and from which the weak fall off. Many Canadians perceive this to be the situation, and I will deal with this particular issue during my speech.
Before focusing on the economic problems and courses of action we have taken and can take, I would like to point out that members of the House have identified high interest rates, inflation, unemployment, low productivity and foreign ownership as our major enemies. Unlike most hon. members, many Canadians do not see the need to sacrifice one against the other, and I agree with that view.
The Economic Council of Canada concurred with this in its report of October, 1981, and offered two concrete proposals to bring down inflation while at the same time lowering interest rates and lessening the negative impact on unemployment and economic slowdown.
John Kenneth Galbraith also seems to agree on this point and, further, offers different proposals which I will discuss in more detail later.
Turning now to the economy in general, I would like to discuss what I see to be our approach to the macroeconomic and structural aspects of the Canadian economy. The first area is economic measures which have already been taken outside the budget that serve to set the economic framework in which the budget will operate. I support the principle of a strong national government with the necessary tools to face our economic challenges. I do not support the "community of communities" principle espoused by the opposition. I see this principle leading to the further balkanization of our country, resulting in ten fiefdoms fighting common enemies with uncoordinated and often contradictory strategies.
Canada must have a strong national government to direct, co-ordinate and unify our country's attack on our economic problems. Our government has gone a long way toward this goal through the Constitution, the National Energy Program and the energy agreements between the national government and some provinces. The increased revenues from multinationals and the long-term reduced capital outflow have done much
more than any five budgets in the past to enable us to reduce our deficit, thus easing the pressure on interest rates and inflation, as well as helping to balance our current account deficits over the long-term.
The second area that must be considered is the impact of the United States economic strategy. Any Canadian budget is based, to a large degree, on the estimated economic performance of the United States. The United States owns and controls over 60 per cent of the energy and manufacturing sectors of our economy. As well, it is our largest trading partner, with 70 per cent.
President Reagan now concedes that the United States economy is in a recession that, as he put it, "none of us predicted." Let us consider the dramatic changes in the economic policy in the United States since it was first proposed in the 1980 election campaign. In that campaign, President Reagan set forth his platform of massive tax cuts, massive cuts in social spending as advised by David Stockman, a massive decrease in defence spending, monetary restraint, which was a policy advanced by Paul Volker, a balanced budget by 1984, reduced inflation and strengthening of the economy through supply side economics. Even then, many political and economic observers said that the arithmetic did not add up.
What has happened since the election campaign? President Reagan appointed David Stockman as the director of the Office of Management and Budget, or OMB, in the United States. In this capacity, he has control of the United States budget and is a major influence on United States economic and social strategy. This is similar to the role of the Minister of Finance in Canada.
Mr. Stockman's major problem was reconciling President Reagan's contradictory campaign promises of raising defence spending, cutting income taxes and balancing the budget all at once. Mr. Stockman's supply side approach to economics was premised on faith, as he admitted, not on economic factors or economic studies, but on faith.
When President Reagan's economic platform was put into the OMB computer, Mr. Stockman was shocked by the results. It showed that the United States deficit would be $82 billion in 1982 and $116 billion by 1984, a level unprecedented in peacetime. David Stockman realized that if this occurred, the stockmarket would panic, interest rates would go higher and long-term inflation would be a certainty. Therefore, the OMB computer was reprogrammed by supply side economists. Instead of being given the orthodox assumptions of how the economy would behave, it assumed a fast decline in prices and interest rates and a huge increase in productivity. Even when these irresponsible assumptions were fed into the computer- which the United States economy has since shown not to be valid-the deficit still showed $60 billion annually, which was also unprecedented in peacetime.
President Reagan has also promised to increase defence spending by $1.6 trillion over the next five years. This is more than double the annual United States budget. This increased defence spending has resulted in such a massive deficit that
December 7, 1981

there is now excessive monetary restraint, which still leaves unquestionably high interest rates.
David Stockman's most disconcerting admission was that the administration's budget was based on shaky premises which did not add up. He stated:
None of us really understand what's going on with all these numbers. You've got so many different budgets out and so many base lines and such complexity now people are getting from A to B and its not clear how they are getting there. Its not clear how we got there.
This is the man who designed the U.S. budget. Even so, Reagan's economic plan was a political success. It was not a success on Wall Street though. The inflation rate was declining, but Stockman conceded this was due more to good luck with grain harvests and world oil supplies than anything Reagan had done. Stockman's original idea that the dramatic political moves would affect the market's expectations of continued high inflation was wrong. He discussed what had gone wrong in this way:
The defence numbers got out of control and we were doing that whole budget-cutting exercise so frantically. In other words, you were juggling details, pushing people, and going from one session to another, trying to cut housing programs here and rural electric there, and we were doing it so fast we didn't know where we were ending up for sure . .. and it didn't quite mesh. That's what happened. But, you see, for about a month and a half we got away with that because of the novelty of all these budget reductions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sounds like U.S. News and World Report.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite may not understand the importance of the impact of the U.S. economy on the Canadian economy, but it is of significant importance. If we want to understand how our budget operates in this economy, we should be aware of what is happening in the United States.
There was nothing new about Reagan's new Republicanism in which the oil companies win and the poor lose. Stockman said it too. He stated:
Power is contingent... The power of these client groups turned out to be stronger than I realized. The client groups know how to make themselves heard. The problem is, unorganized groups can't play this game.
Stockman's final analysis of the whole mess:
Whenever there are great strains or changes in the economic system it tends to generate crackpot theories, which then find their way into the legislative channels.
I have a number of points to make on the fiasco of President Reagan's program on which the U.S. budget director has reported.
First, the importance of Canada gaining control of its own economy through Canadianization with the National Energy Program and through the Foreign Investment Review Agency is underlined. However, the timing of this is also important, as will be discussed later. We must use economic strategy increasingly and tools that target on domestic inflation, interest rates and economic growth.
We cannot assume any positive impact on our economy from the United States. Adjustments in our policy may have to be considered in light of this new information that David
The Budget-Mr. Lang
Stockman has given us since our own budget was outlined. However, it is a good sign that Mr. Stockman has had the courage to tell it like it is, which may generate enough political pressure on President Reagan to get his act together.
The third area I will consider with respect to the economy in general is monetary policy. The responsibility of the Bank of Canada, and I quote Governor Bouey:
-is to discharge its parliamentary mandate, to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation.
Until now we have seen monetary policy being used as the bulwark of anti-inflationary methods by most countries of the western industrialized world. Paul Volker of the U.S. Federal Reserve Board has been the pacesetter, and again we have seen the dramatic impact of U.S. measures in Canada. Our interest rates follow theirs like a slow but persistent tracking dog, not getting up to the same peaks or as deep into the valleys but nevertheless always on track.
It is of interest to note Governor Bouey's comments on this in the 1980 annual report of the Bank of Canada. It states this:
Although control over the rate of monetary expansion is an essential component of an effective anti-inflationary policy it should not be the only element. If it is left to carry the whole load it may, to be effective, have to involve such high interest rates as to be very disruptive to the functioning of the economy. Very high interest rates have an uneven impact on the economy, affecting particularly those areas of activity that typically involve the use of large amounts of credit, as for example, house building. The slowing of inflation will be accomplished with much less economic and social strain if policies elsewhere in the economy help the process.
Despite these statements we see that the recent fall in Canadian interest rates has been impeded by the Bank of Canada. This is inconsistent with the bank's own guides to action, the value of the Canadian dollar and the growth in money supply as measured by Ml.
If this continues, it will hold interest rates unnecessarily high and deepen the recession that is already causing widespread lay-offs. The constituents in my riding are well aware of this.
Governor Bouey used to state that a strong dollar meant that we could lower interest rates, but he is now letting our dollar rise relative to all other currencies. The other determinant of interest rate policy has been the growth of the money supply. Instead of letting the money supply grow by up to 4 to 8 per cent per year, the target announced, the Bank of Canada has allowed no growth at all in the past 12 months. In fact, the Ml money supply has declined by $1 billion from October 1980, from $25.2 billion to $24.2 billion.
The Bank of Canada itself has said the minimum to keep our economy growing without inflation is $26 billion, or we are short of $1.8 billion. Hence, the Bank of Canada has the elbow room to ease up on tight money allowing some increase in growth and decreased interest rates. When money is kept this tight, it means that interest rates are higher than necessary and are only exacerbating inflation.
I would now like to consider the budget in relation to the economy. Looking at general economic policy and the budget, we can see a number of adjustments that have validity and can

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Lang
be made to improve our prospects. First, considering restraint, we have seen that there has been excessive monetary restraint and that we can increase our money supply without any inflationary impact, leading to an immediate decrease in pressure on interest rates as well as increased employment and productivity in the short term.
Next I would like to consider expenditure control. I have received numerous representations from my constituents on the importance of expenditure. In this area, the government has a rate of expenditure growth of 16.3 per cent for this fiscal year. Apart from public debt charges, the total dollar amount charges that will be spent are less than the amount forcast in the budget of October, 1980.
The government has had to pay an additional $2 billion in public debt charges because of higher interest rates. It is this increase, not new spending programs, which accounts for the unexpected increase in our expenditures to 16.3 per cent.
The budget sets out a program for steady reduction of the deficit. Financial requirements are expected to decline from $9.8 billion in 1981-82 to $6.6 billion in 1982-83. Most important, financial requirements are less than anticipated in the October 1980 budget. They are $1.2 billion less in 1981-82 and $1.8 billion less in 1982-83.
The second major principle of the budget is equity. There is little question that the major inequity we have in our economy today is high interest rates. The increased revenues from the multinational oil companies as a result of the energy agreement as well as fiscal measures discussed above are in the right direction in terms of alleviating pressure on interest rates.
Aid has been targeted to home owners with mortgages coming due, small businesses and farmers. These groups have borne an inequitable burden of the fight against inflation. My constituents inform me that this aid is not having the desired impact, partly due to poor co-operation from the banks. Further pressure on the banks is required. It is important to note that an excessive increase in bank profits due to higher interest rates is not an equitable situation, as clearly they are not bearing any of the burden in the fight against inflation. In fact, they appear to be profiting from it.
Considering equity further, we have the suggestions of more direct price-cost control advocated by John Kenneth Galbraith. Adding to this adjusted monetary and fiscal policies, as he suggests, enables us to deal with the cost-push component of inflation with considerably less negative impact on interest rates. Furthermore, he points out that decreasing interest rates frees up capital for industrial modernization and economic growth. Just as important, in terms of equity, employment prospects are dramatically improved.
I am disappointed that we have not seen more constructive alternatives put forward by the official opposition. Is it because, in their own self interest to gather power, they are afraid to propose constructive measures that will always have a downside to them and hence lay the opposition open to criticism? Nowhere in this debate have I heard direct price cost
controls being discussed, and despite both their merits and detractions, they have been used with varying degrees of success against cost push inflation since World War II. They have been used by many countries such as the U.S., Britain, Switzerland, West Germany and Canada.
I do not put it forward as a panacea, Mr. Speaker. However, I ask a number of questions. Is it wise to abandon completely the major bulwark of anti-inflationary policy in the past, a policy that has proven by experience in many countries to be at least partially successful. On adopting monetary restraint to deal with excessive total aggregate demand, the new and as yet unproven anti-inflationary theory, should we abandon totally the cost push theories of inflation and direct price cost controls? Is not the inequity of excessive monetary restraint, which cuts aggregate demand through high interest rates, decreasing economic growth and unemployment, greater than the inequity of direct price cost controls? Should we not consider the pros and cons of adding direct price cost controls to monetary and fiscal restraint by taking some of the burden off monetary restraint, which would allow further output and hence higher employment, as well as lower interest rates? By dealing with domestic inflation more directly, we can also lessen the negative impact of U.S. policies. Although, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) pointed out in the budget, we cannot insulate ourselves from the United States, nevertheless, we must face the reality, as enunciated by David Stockman, that unless the United States takes dramatic steps to control defence spending or totally changes its program, both of which are unlikely, the U.S. will continue with stagflation, volatile interest rates and inflationary pressures for some time to come.
Hence, I believe, further consideration of direct price cost controls is essential, as well as being more equitable in terms of dealing with the inequities of high interest rates and high unemployment.
Another aspect of equity in the budget is the new tax reform measures. Again, I have had numerous representations about the closure of tax expenditure loopholes. Many of my constituents feel that, in some measure, the Department of Finance has miscalculated the impact on the economy and individuals. As well, they feel that in addition to catching those who are abusing these tax loopholes, the middle class, the productive sector of our society, those who are working for a living, will be hard hit and that there will be tremendous discouragement through the efforts of working and saving. The Minister of Finance has indicated that appropriate adjustments will be made to the withdrawal of these tax incentives to ensure that the desired impact is obtained. This should also deal with other concerns that have been raised in regard to loss of high risk venture capital necessary to junior Canadian oil and gas companies as well as to new high technology industries.
Now let us consider economic growth, the third major principle of the budget. We have seen that we do not have to wait for inflation to be brought under control before allowing the economy to grow.
December 7, 1981

The above measures, past experience, as well as economic theory, allow for growth associated with increased capital formation and productivity, while protecting against inflationary growth. Thus, we can move on with implementing the strategy contained in the budget's document "Economic Development for Canada in the Eighties".
I should like to highlight briefly some of these points. First, the start-up of the megaprojects and other natural resource industries; second, measures for increasing industrial investment, as well as research and development; third, facilitating increased transportation capacity, particularly in export trade expansion in grain, coal, fertilizers and forest products; fourth, increased export trade by implementing the strategy contained in the budget for export development and by lower value of the Canadian dollar relative to other currencies; and fifth, facilitating the education and training of human resources, particularly for application in microelectronics technology and megaprojects.
The last area of consideration is the international structural aspects of our economy. Most Canadians are aware of the large degree of foreign ownership and control of both the energy and non-energy sectors of our economy. In fact, our economy is often referred to as a branch plant economy. The government has recognized this with the Canadianization aspects of the National Energy Program and with the Foreign Investment Review Agency. I believe that the government has also recognized that the pace and timing of gaining further control of our economy is critically important. We must be aware of the problems of capital outflow, current account deficit, decreased foreign investment and retaliatory measures, which are threatened by the U.S. either directly through the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade or, indirectly, which can result from moving too quickly on re-owning our economy, or which can result from the inappropriate timing of these measures, such as in times of economic stress.
Another aspect in considering structure in the economy is tax reform, which was briefly discussed earlier. The government has introduced measures to increase tax equity. This is welcomed. Again, we must be aware of the timing and pace of these reforms so as not to introduce further stress to an already embattled economy. There are dangers to decreasing business investment, decreasing capital formation, decreasing employment and decreasing incentives for high risk venture capital.
The incentive for risk-taking, increased productivity, and the entrepreneurial spirit must not be hampered. The Minister of Finance has indicated the importance of ensuring a positive impact on the economy with respect to tax reform. He has also indicated an openness to adjustments where further equity can be obtained.
I have already discussed in the House my concern with tax on unrealized accrued income on life insurance savings and the impact on dependants, jobs and business investments that are involved.
Again on the international level, Mr. Speaker, because of the failure of the U.S. approach so far, this places even more
The Budget-Mr. Oberle
pressure on Canada to take a leadership role in a truly equitable fight against inflation. It is not unusual to have economists split on what the economic future holds; but it is unusual when the director of the economic strategy of the major economy in the free world, the United states economy, indicates that his strategy has been a failure. Budget Director, David Stockman, has done exactly this. Again, I am hopeful that this admission in itself will produce changes in the U.S. policy; but as yet we have no evidence of this change. It is incumbent upon Canada to take a leadership role in showing that inflation can be beaten, unemployment reduced and economic growth proceed on the basis of output and productivity.
For the western world to go through a recessionary period, with the tremendous social damage and inequity involved, would be truly devastating, particularly if the battle against inflation is not won. This would seriously endanger any attempts to control inflation in the future. People are hurting in this fight against inflation and they expect positive results for their sacrifice.
United States policies have endangered the probability of positive results. This is yet another impelling reason for Canada to approach inflation in terms of targeting more closely on domestic inflation, as opposed to targeting on inflation as a whole in Canada. There is little we can do about foreign inflation, Mr. Speaker, other than setting an example of how to beat inflation. I believe this can be done with the economic framework we now have and the economic measures discussed above. By recording success in controlling domestic inflation, which again can be recorded with the GNE deflator, as opposed to the CPI, we can instil a sense of confidence in Canadians, and, by our success, give an example to other countries in the western industrialized world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not help but be somewhat amused when I listened to the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) speak about the budget, not so much our budget but that of the United States. If I were a Liberal these days, I would probably prefer to speak about Mr. Stockman and his budget much more than I would about the document we are discussing in the House this evening. I wonder whether the hon. member knows that inflation in the United States is 5 per cent below that of our own, that interest rates are 5 per cent below ours, and that all signs point toward the fact that the Americans are indeed in much better control of their economy than we could ever hope to be, particularly after this budget.
I doubt whether there has ever been a budget that was more universally rejected, that was so off the target as this one. It is fair and equitable only in the sense that the devastation is universal. The minister has not forgotten anyone in his compulsory restraint program. Our offices are flooded with mail daily. Our constituents are calling this document cynical, cruel and callous. It was received with disgust, dismay and outright anger. The only theme is a major attack on the private sector and more government intervention in every sphere of economic

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Oberle
activity. It is a frontal attack on the middle class, on small business and on the farm sectors, and it robs the poor.
There is no better example than the one I must cite where the government, expecting and planning for a massive increase in unemployment, is intending in its budget to impose a measure which will tax severance pay that companies pay the employees they have to lay off.
The message to us is to reduce our expectations. The minister in charge of housing interprets that to mean that we must learn to sit on orange crates again. The ownership of a home or the affordability to rent decent shelter is no longer a social right under the government but a privilege which is conferred on the deserving by their government. Those who have a few dollars to invest are taxed on money they have not yet earned or may never earn. In the past, farmers were allowed to average income from a farm sale, which is the only profit they would have made in their lives. Now they must pay tax on all their income the first year. Even life insurance premiums, unrealized accrued income, will be taxed. They are calling that a closing of the loophole!
Why do they do these things? It is quite obvious to anyone who has sat across from these social engineers for the last ten years that Canadians should not be greedy and save for old age; after all, their government will look after them from cradle to grave! Why should they save money in life insurance? Why should they build up assets or equity in farmland? There is no need to do that because the government looks after them when they are old! It appears that the government, having realized that conventional textbook measures are ineffective in solving the stubborn and chronic problems of inflation, unemployment and high interest rates, has only made the problem worse. But the government has not yet come to understand why these conventional measures are no longer effective. The normal tinkering to stimulate economic growth or to slow it down has not worked. The reason for all this is quite obvious to even the most casual observer. The government is overlooking the facts that private sector activity in the economy is no longer the most dominant factor and that the public sector is not playing by the same rules. For instance, how can we expect to bring down interest rates when the government competes in the marketplace totally unrestrained, as if there were no tomorrow?
The banks are blamed for the fact that thousands of businesses go bankrupt and people lose their homes. Yet any cash the banks may have had to invest in Small Business Development Bonds or mortgages was skimmed off by the latest issue of Canada Savings Bonds which the government guaranteed at 5 per cent above market rates. They are forgetting that the public sector now leads in every sphere of economic activity. Energy prices, indiscriminately set by governments, are a major cost to all industries and all individuals, so are other government-regulated or controlled services such as transportation, communications and postal rates. For example, postal rates have seen an increase of 60 per cent. The public sector continues to lead in wage and salary settlements and spends money as if there were no tomorrow. One of the themes of the
budget is restraint-restraint, indeed! It would not matter how well the lesson contained in the Liberal budget were received or how much the average Canadian restrained his demand on the economy. Unless the government begins to practise what it preaches, things can only get worse. The message in this budget and all indications from the initial response to it indicate that things will get much worse.
The financial wizards of the Liberal government all lament the fact that our productivity has fallen way behind that of other industrial nations, and claim that to be a major contributing factor to our economic ills. I agree, but when was a planned and controlled economy ever productive? I should like the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to tell me of one example where a government-controlled economy ever produced anything but inefficiency, waste and shortages, and particularly shortages in people's confidence in themselves. I see nothing in the budget to restore any of the confidence we have already lost, I see no economic renewal in the budget at all.
Last week one of my colleagues said in the House that we could see a move toward a collective farm sector. It was during the question period and it brought spontaneous laughter from the other side. I wonder how much longer farmers will continue to produce cheap food below the cost of production just because the government tells them to. The only sectors in the agricultural industry which are still viable are those that operate under the control of supply management through marketing boards. It is quite apparent that the beef and red meat industries will have to be organized under such a scheme if they are to survive. I am philosophically opposed to marketing boards, but they are the only thing which will keep farmers alive. It is direct control, and it only works domestically. We have only to look at the Milk Marketing Board. We used to sell a lot of cheese to the European Economic Community; we do not any longer because the marketing board has taken care of that. It is not because free enterprise no longer works but because one cannot just intervene a little in the economy, just like one cannot be a little pregnant. Once one starts, one must go all the way. All the way is what tumbles around in the cupboard of the former brain kitchen of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-the head of Jim Coutts. I will tell the House what he said. He shed his obligation to secrecy just recently. He is now at large, away from the loony bin. He is so convinced of the virtues of the economic order to which he and his former boss subscribe that he is testing his theories on the public platform. He competed in an election and he made a speech to a Liberal convention. He is not content with government ownership of the energy sector alone, even though modern day socialists no longer believe, as did Karl Marx, that the state must own the tools and machines of production. They think, rightly so, that if we control and own the energy which drives the machines and own and control the resources which are fed through the machine, the rest can well be left to the proletariat. But Jim Coutts wants to go further. He wants the state to own the lumber industry. Would that be good news to lumber people? He wants the high tech business controlled and
December 7, 1981

owned by government, he wants the agricultural sector in some way controlled by the government. Some of the anger which has fed back to our offices was a result of the fact that we overlooked that some Canadians think they have a right to the ownership of their property. The rejection of the budget has something to do with this, because people fear and mistrust those social reformers opposite. They actually thought that Jim Coutts could have his way and could assume complete control and ownership of our farm industry some day! Fortunately 'the people of Spadina opted for a somewhat less radical and dangerous representative of the social democrats. It is said that there is a difference between the Liberals and the social democrats; at least the people of Spadina believe that.
One of the great features of our system is the right of the electorate to receive as much punishment as it keeps asking for. My advice to anyone who has difficulty understanding the theme of the budget is to read it in conjunction with the speech that Jim Coutts delivered to the Liberal convention. That will put it in better focus. It is a giant step forward, a planned economy, not much different from that which operates in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Jim Coutts and his former boss believe that the failure of the Soviets to feed themselves has nothing to do with the way their economic order is arranged but has something to do with the 53 consecutive crop failures experienced in the Soviet Union. The Lord must not be smiling at our friends behind the Iron Curtain.
What this budget represents is an inevitable consequence of 12 years of pursuing the socialist notion of taking from each according to his ability and giving to each according to his need. That is equity, according to the government.
I always like to refer to the professor of political science from New York who tells his students that in order to understand this concept of socialism they just have to look around the classroom and say to the students who receive 95 per cent in tests, that they should give up some of their marks to those who only achieve 55 per cent. That way, everyone would end up with equal passing marks-about 70 per cent or 75 per cent. That seems fair. After adjusting all the scores, everyone would be equal! The question is, would the student who earns 95 per cent work as hard the following year? Would the student who only received 65 per cent work at all? In fact, quite soon all students would score well below the passing grade. Compulsory assignments and severe punishments would be needed in order to raise the grade of even the most capable to the passing level.
Productivity in our economy has long ago fallen below the passing level. Too many people with great ability have registered themselves among the needy. More and more of us are throwing up our hands, no longer able to bear the load being placed on us.
This budget, sir, is the first of the compulsory assignments and the punishment which is needed to raise the passing grade of our activity-except that it is not going to work. The government will just find someone else to blame. The Minister
The Budget-Mr. Oberle
of Finance tells us that it is the banks that are to blame for businesses, large and small, going under, and for the people who are losing their farms and their homes. Oil price increases are the fault of the multinational corporations.
As I said earlier, it is not possible to intervene just a little bit. It is hardly the fault of the oil companies when the government doubles taxes through order in council and then the price of gasoline and heating oil increases, or when the Bank of Canada increases the prime lending rate. If a government adopts these measures, then it must go all the way and tax excessive profits. That is what the NDP wants to do. It wants to bring in a windfall profits tax. If bank profits can be legislated, then it may be necessary to bring in such a measure.
Jim Coutts wants to go further, however. He wants more nationalization in order to solve the problem completely. I suppose bank employees would have nothing to lose-they would get 17 weeks maternity leave, indexed pensions and all the perks which fall under the security blanket that comes with a public service job. Of course, the banks would not register any more profit and therefore would not have any money to lend to small business in order to create new jobs. But without the need to be accountable to those greedy shareholders, the banks, the oil companies or any other government enterprise would undoubtedly take up the slack by hiring a lot of new people themselves, thereby making life easier for everyone else.
Sir, it is not going to work. I will tell you what the theme of this budget is-it is the same as every other budget since our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) proclaimed his new society.
As Churchill said 40 years ago, you can remove the inherent vice of free enterprise and capitalism, which is the unequal distribution of blessings, and replace it with the inherent virtue of socialism, which is the equal distribution of misery. Even that only works in theory because there really is no misery for those who are on the inside. The socialists always look after themselves.
I sometimes wonder what Liberal members tell their constituents when they go home to lecture them and explain why and how ordinary people should restrain their demands on the economy. I am sure some constituents must ask, "What have you done lately to cut back your own demands, or the government's? What about some of the friends of the party or the higher echelons of the bureaucracy?" What about Mr. Cam-peau, here in Ottawa? He is a builder-is he suffering? Of course not, because the Liberals are looking after him. What about Mr. Bouey, for instance, although one should be fair to him. After all, he only accepted a 9 per cent increase in his salary, although he chastises everyone else for taking as much as 10 per cent or even 12 per cent. Mr. Bouey is one of these neat flow chart people who work with percentages. Such people dominate the public service these days-the social engineers who figure everything in percentages. He got a 9 per cent increase in his salary. This amounted to $9,000 and brought his salary to $104,000 per year. The average Canadian earning $15,000 or $20,000 and asking for a 10 per cent increase will get only $2,000 and end with $22,000 per year.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate, first because it will give me the opportunity to point out the importance of the small business sector for the Canadian economy, and second, because the government has recognized this importance and taken action to promote the development of Canadian small businesses both in the past and in this budget.
Detailed analysis of this budget shows that it contains several provisions to assist small businesses. First, it relies on the many incentives developed by the government in the past to assist small businesses. Second, it contains a series of new measures which will be especially beneficial to small businesses, and finally, it promotes a climate which will promote the development of small and large businesses in Canada.
But what about the base which had already been established? Before the budget, certain tax measures were designed especially for small businesses. Nothing has changed in this regard. These measures are too numerous to list them all, but I would like to mention some of the most important. As everyone knows, there is, of course, the reduced income tax rate for small businesses, which is about 21 per cent lower than that applied to large businesses. This provision means a loss in revenue of $1 billion a year for the Government of Canada.
December 7, 1981

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
