speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the hon. members opposite, who are rarely in great numbers in the House, say that this is nonsense. Perhaps it is nonsense in their opinion to help

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. C. Lapointe
businesses that are experiencing financial hardship, and nonsense also to allow unincorporated businesses to be eligible for this program, because they believe that to assist the Canadian economy only the richer segments of our society need be helped.
Under the Small Business Development Bond program, the Government of Canada will be spending an additional $82 million.
Another provision affecting small business and contributing to the development of this sector, which is one of the objectives of this budget, is the two-year extension on the business corporate surtax. But, as the Minister of Finance stated in his budget speech, small businesses will be exempt from the surtax payable on that part of their income which is eligible for the reduced small business tax rate. This will allow small businesses to save approximately $100 million in income tax over the next two years.
As of 1982, the employer's weekly contribution to the unemployment insurance plan will be reduced by about 9 per cent, which means that the employer's contribution will go down from $2.52 to $2.31. That too, Mr. Speaker, is a measure that the small business community had requested. I think that will allow small businesses to save approximately $75 million a year.
The provisions announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech with respect to small manufacturers will also help the small business community. The federal tax rate on income from manufacturing and processing operations will decrease from 15 to 10 per cent. Under the existing tax provisions, a small business had to separate its eligible manufacturing operations income from all its other income using complicated calculations if its total yearly income was above $50,000. Previously, a corporation which was mainly involved in manufacturing and whose total income did not exceed $50,000 did not have to make these calculations. Now, the budget proposes that a small business which is mainly involved in manufacturing should no longer have to separate its income derived from the manufacturing side of its operation from other revenues to benefit from the reduced tax rates which apply to manufacturing revenues. I think that in addition to reducing paperwork, this measure will make it possible once again for small businesses involved in processing and manufacturing to benefit from a still more beneficial system.
One of the major themes of this budget is equity. It is the underlying theme of the changes made to the manner in which dividends from private businesses are treated. Before this budget, the owner of a private business owned by Canadian interests could be paid by his business an income comparable to that of an executive, without having to pay quite as much in income tax. For instance, the owner of a private corporation could be paid up to $30,000 on which he had to pay only the tax rate applicable to small businesses, that is 25 per cent. The employees and unincorporated businessmen paid comparable incomes were subject to an average tax rate of 35 per cent.
As I indicated earlier, one of the main objectives of the government was to develop a more equitable tax system. That
is why some provisions in the budget are designed to eliminate a certain imbalance. They will make sure that the decision as to whether a business should be incorporated is based on the financial benefits the business stands to gain rather than on mere fiscal considerations. They will make sure also that the tax deductions granted to small businesses are directed to those which are in full expansion and need them most. There is a third reason, Mr. Speaker, why this budget is beneficial to small businesses. It will foster an economic climate in which all Canadian businesses will begin to thrive as the worldwide recession dies down. I mean, of course, the considerable effort which the government has made in this budget to reduce its deficits and its borrowings. As my colleague the Minister of Finance suggested, this effort will alleviate the pressures exerted on the loan markets, reduce the interest rates and leave more room for borrowers seeking funds. The budget is a step in the right direction for this government which is constantly trying to slow down the growth of its spending, leave more room for the private sector and promote entrepreneurship, while assuming its responsibility for leadership and assistance.
I did not mention the many other means which are available to provide financial assistance to small businesses. I am thinking of the Federal Business Development Bank with a lending and borrowing capability of over $2 billion, which helps out more than 40,000 businesses. I am thinking also of the risk capital of the Federal Business Development Bank which has invested more than 40 million dollars in over 150 manufacturing companies in this country. In addition, there is, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the Small Businesses Loans Act pursuant to which 1.4 billion loans are guaranteed by the Canadian government to 24,000 businesses. I could mention many more programs, such as the National Research Council Programs, the Industrial Research Assistance Program, the Small Business Development Program, the Regional Economic Expansion Department program, the Suppliers' Establishment Funds, the Supply and Services Department Program.
Mr. Speaker, considering this wide range of opportunities, it is obvious that over the last few years and even now in the present budget the government has done its very best to aid small businesses and has promoted original policies, as I mentioned earlier, when I compared our fiscal system to those of countries similar to our own. The present budget respects this commitment and is an efficient way of helping small Canadian businesses build a better future for themselves.
I would like to remind hon. members, as the Minister of Finance has mentioned several times in this House, that he is ready to listen to proposals by groups of people and Members of Parliament in order to determine whether or not in some cases certain adjustments may be justified for the sake of equity. As Minister of State for Small Businesses, Mr. Speaker, I shall and do live up to my responsibilities to see to it that all the concerns of small businessmen are brought to the attention of my cabinet colleagues.
December 7, 1981

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take advantage of the few minutes I have left to address another topic which also concerns and affects small businesses, more particularly in Ontario and Quebec. I would like to deal for awhile with the new Canadian policy on behalf of the shoe industry. I would like to quote from a paper which was presented or read at the Quebec National Assembly, during the presentation of the Parizeau Budget in 1979:
The traditional textile, clothing, shoe and furniture industries which in 1977 had lost 20,000 jobs and were in some cases threatened with total elimination, were saved by the adoption of radical policies. The federal government agreed to pursue a strict and responsible policy of quota imposition for three to four years to protect three of those industries. And the Quebec government removed the sales tax from those four areas for a year ... it is most important that we agree on the objective. For three years the governments will give an exceptional assistance to those traditional industries. We shall do everything possible to reach a specific objective, which is to make them competitive within three years with their American and Western European counterparts. We will not ask them to compete with Taiwan or Korea. That would not be possible. But I must give those industries the solemn warning that, at the end of those three years, they cannot expect an extension of this exceptional government help. It is up to them to undertake right now the work of reorganization and modernization which is necessary to their survival.
Mr. Speaker, this speech by the Minister of Finance in Quebec is exactly what we have sought to implement after four years of protective measures on behalf of the shoe industry.
Total imports during the period from 1977 to 1981 increased by 9.2 million pairs of footwear compared with 1975. More than 80 per cent of that disastrous increase consisted of footwear made of materials other than leather. Of the other 20 per cent, leather footwear, more than two thirds came from both developed and state-trading countries. So, a cursory look at those figures prove clearly, Mr. Speaker, that the sad state of affairs with regard to low-production-cost countries is caused by a sharp increase in footwear imports other than leather and cannot be blamed on increased imports of leather footwear from those countries. Since 1977, the situation has changed considerably. For instance, the value of the Canadian dollar is no longer what it was and Canadian producers have improved their productivity, thanks not only to the steps taken by the Quebec government, as mentioned by the Quebec Minister of Industry and Tourism, but also to the restructuration program of the government of Canada.
The Canadian leather and man-made fabric shoe industry is protected, moreover, by a 24.4 per cent rate of value for duty advances in the case of nine countries, including Italy and Brazil; in addition, it is still possible to resort to the normal protection of compensatory rights and anti-dumping rules as provided for in federal legislation. The Anti-dumping Tribunal, which made the study of the industry on which our new policy is based, indicates on page 112 of its report that it is now satisfied that the Canadian footwear industry is now able to compete with the imports from developing economies and state-trading countries.
In 1980, Canadian producers had over 70 per cent of the domestic leather footwear market, industrialized countries 20 per cent and underdeveloped countries 10 per cent. Among the latter, Brazil represented almost half the imports. With regard
The Budget-Mr. C. Lapointe
to that country, the Tribunal recognizes in its report and concludes on page 113 that, "the necessity of special measures of protection in the case of Brazil is somewhat less urgent as imports from that source are subjected to a 50 per cent advance for duty". And this, Mr. Speaker, in addition to the 24.4 per cent rate on any imported footwear. Again, as far as Brazil is concerned, Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago, it levied a 15 per cent export tax on that footwear. Now considering the small share of the leather footwear market held by other underdeveloped countries, you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that it would be almost impossible to justify any unilateral action to our trade partners, even if there were some international mechanisms such as, for example, the multi-fiber agreement on textile and clothing now in effect. It would not be possible at all to justify such an exception under our GATT agreements.
As for footwear other than leather on which we imposed a quota, the Tribunal concluded also, on page 123, that the greater part of the increase in imports from underdeveloped countries would be absorbed by footwear other than leather, and that Canadian manufacturers especially would suffer. That prejudice could be ascribed to substitution.
Now, the decision of the government of Canada to impose quotas on footwear other than leather is based on real statistics and on the findings of the Anti-dumping Tribunal. In addition, it must also be kept in mind that if we had imposed quotas on leather footwear, which would have affected mostly our trading partners of the European Economic Community and the United States, it is quite obvious that many Quebec and Ontario manufacturers of leather footwear already exporting much of their production to those markets, would also have been subjected to retaliatory measures and would have been unable to export their footwear to those markets. With this new restructuration and modernization program for which we have earmarked $17 million to bring special assistance to footwear manufacturers so they will expand their export activities by closing our markets to all but leather footwear, I think we can hope that the workers and the manufacturers will be able to get a handle on the new situation and develop a much more dynamic and much more competitive footwear industry. In any event, before the end of the week my colleague the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Bussieres) and myself will meet with the footwear manufacturers and the spokesmen for the labour force in that industry.
I wanted to take the opportunity offered in this speech to clear up the situation on that subject because we have been getting political flak from the government of Quebec which has been saying that the footwear industry will go belly up. I also wanted to demonstrate the originality of our tax system for small Canadian businesses with all the new measures contained in the budget we are studying now, and that small Canadian businesses will continue to be the backbone of our economic development and that, for the government of Canada, it will remain the most important sector of our economy.

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Althouse

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this budget was brought down, I had a very modest list of items which I had hoped would be in it. These items applied to agriculture, which is my area of concern. I thought we might see some much needed improvement in funding for stabilization programs in the agricultural community.
During this International Year of the Disabled Persons, I hoped that there would be at least a minor bow in recognition of that fact by providing for some equality in the application of the Income Tax Act for people who are mentally handicapped. There are families of mentally handicapped people who do not have the same kind of tax options which are available to families of physically disabled people.
I had sent letters to the various ministers involved in the hope that there would be some recognition of this situation during this year of the disabled and that it would be corrected. It would not cost the people of Canada very much and it would, in fact, give some recognition to those families with mentally disabled people who are sometimes faced with a great financial cost.
I had hoped that there would be some increased funding to the Farm Credit Corporation through the introduction of a means of recycling the funds which go from one farming generation to the next. I would have liked to have seen a method whereby the farmer who was selling the farm would be allowed to reinvest his money in the Farm Credit Corporation bond at a reduced tax rate to encourage the recycling of money which, in turn, would be more available since the Farm Credit Corporation at the present time supplies only between 5 per cent and 10 per cent of the required funds for refinancing.
I had also hoped that some means would be provided in this budget to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to provide for additional sources of funding, either from private or government sources. With the exception of $45 million, that too did not happen.
Since we have just experienced a fairly heavy tax regime under the National Energy Program and the energy agreements between the federal government and the producing provinces, I had hoped that the tax increases would not be too great. There are some sectors of our economy, such as the banks and oil companies which are making tremendous profits from the high interest rates, and I would like to have seen a tax leveled on these windfall profits. That did not happen either.
I thought that it might have been time for the recognition of the workers who are not working under a union contract and have to supply most of their own equipment for their trade, whether it be carpentry, plumbing or farming; that there would be some allowance for them to write off part of their tools as part of their jobs. That was not in the budget either.
One of the main farm planks in the Liberal Party campaign during the last election was a change in the valuation day for farmland from the end of 1971 to the end of 1974. This was
one of the few planks in the Liberal Party platform, and I was extremely distressed to see that it was not included in the budget. Since there was no change to the valuation day, no changes in the Farm Credit Corporation, no monies for the stabilization program I was beginning to wonder where the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had been when the proposals for the budget were being drawn up. Those are some of the things which were not provided for in the budget.
What we did get were changes to the income-averaging annuity program which were not particularly welcomed in the farming community. I believe that these changes were aimed more at the professional athletes, perhaps entertainers and presidents of large corporations who receive large sums of money on the termination of contracts. In these areas the changes to the income-averaging annuity program contract may have some element of fairness because these people are not at the end of their careers. Most of them will again take jobs and be part of the economy. However, as this provision applies to retiring farmers, I maintain that the effect, on balance, is unfair.
The provision for income-averaging annuity has been beneficial to farmers since it first came into effect in 1972 because it was offered in recognition of the fact that while farmers may not be producing very much in the way of income tax payments during their careers-I will elaborate on this point later-they do find themselves facing retirement with fairly large sums of money in some cases, and this income-averaging annuity contract allowed the farmer to average his income on a forwarding basis, thus spreading the effects of that income, which had been accumulated sometimes up to 50 years, over the ensuing five to 10 years. This protection is not longer available to the farmer.
The effective elimination of the IAAC, if we can use that short term, will probably produce a tendency for farmers to sell less land and in smaller parcels, which will not make it any easier for the rest of the community continuing to farm. With this tendency, it also means that these sales will take place over a number of years in an effort to effect the same kind of tax averaging which was available under the IAAC program. The more worrisome effects of the program's elimination are the different reactions to this from the operators of small and medium-sized farms as opposed to the reaction from farmers with larger operations. The farmers who sold their farms in 1981 with the understanding that they would be able to use the income averaging annuity program to spread their tax burden are especially affected by this budget. These people were caught on November 12. I have received phone calls from several who have been caught in the unhealthy position of having sold their land under an agreement of sale in order to spread the income over the next four or five years. As of budget date, they will have to consider all of the sale as income this year, even though they will not receive the income until five years down the road. They will have to pay tax on that income.
December 7, 1981

Most of those who called face the prospect of having to borrow money to pay the tax. They will have no money left to purchase a house or even to pay rent on one so that they will have a place to live in their retirement years. This is simply because of the manner in which this program has been implemented.
Another change in the income tax as it affects farmers is in the capital gains reserve. As of November 12, after the budget, sellers of land will no longer be able to average the payment of income tax on capital gains when the purchaser makes payment to the vendor over a number of years. I discussed some of the problems by using the example of the man who had sold his land and will receive payments over five years who finds himself in the unenviable position of having no money to pay his tax and no money for the next year and a half of his retirement.
This kind of financing will probably be wiped out. About 10 per cent of the sales that now take place are financed on vendor-purchase agreements. That may not sound like much, but I remind hon. members the Farm Credit Corporation finances less than 10 per cent of the land transactions that take place in this country. Therefore, we are talking about a program that will affect more land transactions than the Farm Credit Corporation and will affect them very negatively.
The budget tends to create a regressive tax system in relation to capital gains rollovers when parents transfer farmland to children. The Minister of Agricuture takes great joy in pointing out that the rollover provision is still there, and it is. Flowever, the effect will be different, depending on the income and the size of the farming operation that is being rolled over.
Two or three accountants have brought examples which indicate that the small or medium-sized farmer, because he has no other source of income to retire with, is forced to sell his small holding at full or nearly full market value. This means he will be paying capital gains tax on that property. It also means that his sons, daughters or grandchildren will have to pay full or nearly full market value for that property. At today's interest rates, it creates a very difficult situation.
The larger operation, because of being able to generate more cash flow and higher net incomes, finds it possible to turn over some, if not all, of the land at the V-day value. On the larger operations we can see where the rollover will apply, and no capital gains tax collected. The next generation will not be forced to pay as high a price for the total assets for which they will be working.
The net result shoult not be too surprising because it is a consistent theme of this budget. The net result is a regressive tax, a tax that falls most heavily on the lower-income people, those with less assets than the amount of tax that falls on those with more assets and higher incomes.
Other changes to the tax laws as they affect farmers in this budget have to do with the Small Business Bond and Small Business Development Bond. The Small Business Development Bonds have been extended. We have a new instrument, the
The Budget-Mr. Althouse
small business bond, which is now available for unincorporated farms, small businesses, fishermen, and will be available as of November 12. The budget states it is available for farms or businesses in financial difficulty. The program may be used after December 31 until the end of 1982. That is what the budget states.
A week ago last Friday I asked the Minister of Agriculture when the regulations and description as to who would be eligible for these bonds would be published. He told me they would be available next week. A week has passed. To date the banks do not have any guidelines as to who is eligible for the small business bond and who is not. Farmers in dire straits have been contacting their bankers. Some will have their land placed in receivership and in the hands of the sheriff before the end of this month, and to date there is still no action on this aspect of the budget. We have the small business bond promised in the budget, but no action. As long as there is no description of who is eligible and who is not, the proposal and offer are of no use to anyone.
The last change in the budget to affect farmers is the changes to the capital cost allowance. To give some idea of the effect, I will run through a brief description of a possible purchase.
Suppose a farmer purchases a $80,000 used tractor and receives $50,000 for his trade-in. The difference he must pay is $30,000. Prior to the budget, he would have shown an acquisition of $80,000 and a disposal of $50,000 in his Class 10 assets on his capital cost schedules, which depreciates at 30 per cent. In other words, from this transaction he would gain $9,000 of capital cost allowance, 30 per cent of $30,000.
After the budget, he would show an acquisition of $80,000. However, he can only depreciate the asset at the new rate of 15 per cent, which would be equivalent to $12,000. In addition, he would have to deduct his trade-in at 30 per cent of $50,000, which equals $15,000. Therefore, he has lost the difference between $15,000 and $12,000, or $3,000 of capital cost allowance because of the new budget.
The loss is even worse than that. Prior to the budget he could show an increase of $9,000. Now he has to show an additional $3,000. His loss in relation to the capital cost allowance schedule is $12,000. Assuming a 35 per cent tax bracket, it is costing the farmer $4,200 in tax to trade one tractor in for another.
I do not think there is very much incentive for a farmer to trade in his equipment. There is no incentive to take the equipment off the lots of dealers. Dealer inventories are increasing at a rapid rate. At today's interest rates, this will have a very negative effect on those small businessmen supplying farm equipment.
Prior to the budget we were seeing a tremendous number of lay-offs in the farm equipment Field. Factories are closing and workers are being laid off right across the country. International Harvester, one of the largest farm equipment manufacturers, now faces the prospect of going into receivership. Massey-Ferguson faced the same problem last year. White

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Althouse
Farm Equipment was refinanced, went bankrupt and was revitalized over the past year. This aspect of the budget will worsen the prospects for the farm equipment industry and employment in that industry. I think that when one looks at the situation in agriculture, had the minister been able to convince the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) of the true state of affairs in agriculture, I am sure it would not have received such short shrift in the budget. There must be some understanding on the government side that there is a lot of money in agriculture or that there is some ability to pay higher taxes, because the government certainly did levy higher taxes on the farm sector. I think this is a misconception. I would refer government members to a very small booklet entitled "Agricultural Facts". It does not take long to read. It has all the data laid out in very simple terms. In that booklet it shows that net farm incomes in Canada in 1973 were $3.3 billion. It was the same in 1980.
Over the same period of time, output in agriculture increased two and a half times, and yet incomes remained virtually the same. If one converts the income in 1980 to 1973 dollars, the net income has decreased almost by half. It is $1.74 billion instead of $3.3 billion. Prospects for 1981 are supposed to be slightly better. They are expecting that it may hit $4 billion this year, an increase of about 12 or 15 per cent. The outlook for 1982 is that it will decrease to $3.4 billion.
While net incomes in agriculture have deteriorated, if one takes into consideration the inflationary effects, productivity has still increased. Even using 1973 dollars, productivity has increased. Agriculture is one of the few sectors of this economy that is more than pulling its weight in terms of productivity versus income received. The thanks they get for it are extra taxes. 1 do not think that is acceptable in terms of fighting inflation; it is not acceptable in terms of equity of taxation. It makes absolutely no sense to me, Mr. Speaker.
When we look at the effects of the budget on agriculture, we have to ask ourselves why the Minister of Finance has introduced this kind of budget. He has told us that he is trying to fight inflation. How is he fighting inflation? By reducing government deficits, he says. He is hoping to increase taxes and decrease spending, thereby reducing the deficit. The minister's economic theory is that because he is doing these things, ' inflation will drop. I think that is an invalid theory.
I should like to spend a few moments now reviewing some of the reasons for reaching this conclusion. I will simply go back to the historic statistics and try to find some rationale for that kind of theory. If the theory has any legitimacy, it should show up in the statistics over the past.
When we go back to the early 1930s, we see the 1930 to 1935 federal budgets had six straight deficits, and not just little deficits but deficits equivalent to $25 billion in today's dollars. What happened to the price level during this time when government spending was in a whirlwind state? Price levels dropped by 26 per cent over that six-year period. They dropped, while government deficits were at an all-time high.
Right after that period during the Second World War, government budget deficits were equivalent to $75 billion in today's dollars. The price level rose about one per cent a year. It is not true that the elimination of budget deficits ends inflation. There was no deficit in 1973. The federal government had a surplus. Along with the surplus budget, in 1973 there also happened to have been the highest rate of inflation we have had for the past 20 years. In 1974 we followed it with an even larger surplus; and the inflation rate rose even higher. I do not see any correlation between budgets and inflation, deficits and inflation.
The other reason for the kind of fiscal policy that this government is embarking upon is to get rid of the burden of the national debt. Today it stands at roughly $100 billion. This year the federal government will have to pay about $15 billion in interest on that debt. Approximately one fifth of the debt is held by the Bank of Canada, which is wholly government-owned and, each year, hands over to the government all the money that it takes at the end of the year, over and above that amount. Of the remaining $80 billion in bonds, $70 billion is held by Canadians. It remains in the country. The government paid them $11 billion, but it is spent within the country.
I maintain that as long as the money is used to produce productive assets, it is an asset to the economy and not a liability. Spending is considered that way even by the economists to my right. As long as it is in the private sector, then in economic theory I see no reason that it should make any difference if it is spent in the public sector, so long as it is spent on productive assets.
In the end, when one finishes doing the arithmetic, one is left with about $9 billion of the $100 billion, $8 billion of which Canadian bondholders had left after tax and was not lost to Canada; and they are fellow Canadians. The real burden of the debt to Canada was about $1 billion which is the approximate cost of maintaining the $8 to $10 billion that is held by foreigners.
That money, which had to be raised from the people of Canada and paid out, went to foreigners. The real burden of that so-called burdensome debt to the country is the amount that we paid to foreigners. We need an economic policy that attempts to gain more control of our economy. We must concentrate more in the area of ordinary Canadians to overcome any so-called burden, thus improving the economy to the point that it would begin to fight inflation with a will.
In closing, I repeat that I see the agricultural sector as perhaps the only sector that is producing more than it takes from the economy. Because it has been doing that, it has had to suffer low net incomes, family incomes that are as low as $8,000 to $12,000 during the period of time when factory workers are earning $12,000 to $15,000. It has had to borrow money in order to expand its productive plants. Because it has had to do this, the amount of money that is owed by farm people has increased. Because of that, when we get into a period of time such as at present when interest rates are extremely high, it is especially burdensome to the agricultural sector.

This budget did not attack the problem of high interest rates in any real and meaningful way. It provided for a small panacea in the form of the small business bond. Those small business bonds have not been activated in any real sense of the word. Until that happens, there will be absolutely no help for the Canadian agricultural sector. It has been a totally negative kind of budget, a regressive budget and one which I think we should vote against. The minister should start over and discuss with the agricultural people of Canada the kind of things that are required in order for them to stay in business. The minister should discuss with the home owners of this country the kind of programs they need to maintain their homes. The minister should discuss with the unemployed the kinds of programs they need in order to get them working again. It is not time to cut back nor to reduce spending. It is time to create employment to get this economy working at close to full capacity again, instead of at a 60 to 80 per cent capacity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words in this budget debate and, because of allocation of time, I should like first to inform my colleagues of the economic conditions which now prevail in the Sherbrooke area. In the last few years, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion opened a regional office in Sherbrooke where business people of the area could apply for assistance given to small and middle-sized businesses in the queen city of the Eastern Townships. For our area, the opening of this office was a significant step because in the past we had to send all our applications to Montreal. I have indicated to this House, more than once, that we have several institutions of higher learning in our area, namely, Sherbrooke University, Bishop University, the College Champlain, the Sherbrooke College and several other specialized schools and every year too large a number of our young people must leave the Eastern Townships area to go to Montreal or to other places in Quebec as well as outside Quebec, to find work.
This means that we educate them but they go and find jobs somewhere else. This is a very sad situation which should be corrected at once and which should be given the highest priority. This is a collective responsibility which involves the federal government, the provincial government, municipalities, intermediary bodies, the business community and all the people of the Estrie area. We can no longer tolerate this brain drain. The greatest wealth of our area are its people and among them the most skilled are leaving. These young people are a significant asset for our development but because of our industrial structure, because of the lack of investments, and because also of the lukewarm interest shown by governments, including the federal government, it is with sadness that we see a large number of our young people going to other places in Quebec and in Canada. Several steps were taken the last year,
The Budget-Mr. Pelletier
and periodically various people take counsel together with regard to the ways and means of co-ordinating the efforts of groups and individuals towards the economic development of Sherbrooke and the Eastern Townships.
About a month ago, a study commissioned by the City of Sherbrooke to a Montreal firm on the Sherbrooke economy, showed that its economic conditions, despite obvious shortcomings, had still a significant potential. This new report considers several aspects of the economic conditions of our area and puts forward suggestions to correct the present situation. Following a rather accurate analysis of the economy of the area, of its healthy and not-so-healthy sectors, in the last chapters of the report possible action and an over-all strategy are suggested foFthe forthcoming years. I sincerely hope that this report will be considered and that as soon as possible we shall come up with a policy that will make it possible to speed up the economic development of that area. For the past decade, studies about Sherbrooke have been undertaken by a variety of people: provincial governments, federal government, university regional agencies and firms of all kinds. I humbly suggest that it is about time-and according to the last report the willingness and the dynamics are there-to launch as of now the economic renewal of the area.
Several opportunities are open to us and personally I think that our approach should be based on a co-ordination of efforts at all levels of government. I sincerely believe that we have available to us several tools which should allow us to make significant progress in the economic development of Sherbrooke. I am thinking in particular of the fact that Sherbrooke University was designated by the federal government as a first-rate centre in electronics. The scientists at Sherbrooke University in electronics have been among the pioneers in this field and this honour with the grants connected to it, should make it possible for the industry of the area to take advantage of the knowledge and the opportunities for development in that leading industry. But there again we will have to make sure that what is done in our area will be of assistance to the small and middle-sized businesses. The University is willing to dispense its knowledge to all those who would like to take advantage of it, and I think that if we could further increase an already well established co-operation between the University and the local economic agents, this could have an extremely positive impact on our area.
It is in the best interests of the economy-oriented organizations in our area to co-ordinate their efforts. Permanent coordination and co-operation should be arranged between the various economic components in the Sherbrooke area. We certainly are not short of economic agencies and organizations to do considerable work. What we need is a co-ordination of our efforts.
Most of our regional economy-oriented organizations have developed plans of action and intervention for the area. We must absolutely make sure that there is a follow-up to our

December 7, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Pelletier
interventions and we must always be careful that what has been gained is thriving and stable. Moreover, not only the new industries that wish to settle in our area but our existing businesses must maintain frequent and numerous contacts so that businessmen, governments at all levels, intermediate bodies, the industrial commission and all organizations involved in economic promotion in our area will work together.
It is impossible during this debate to deal with all the aspects of the question and all the important opportunities available in our area. I will come back to that later. However, for the time being, let me remind you that we have a reasonably progressive service sector, some rather important organizations and the labour force we need to undertake the economic renewal of the area. The authors of the report which I quoted a while ago stated the following in the first paragraph of their document:
Economic growth is for the most part based on the confidence of the business community in its future. Several leaders should not hesitate to assert themselves and to exercise their leadership. The basis of Sherbrooke's economy-
-in spite of some deficiencies however-
-is healthy, in spite of difficult economic conditions. Sherbrooke's economy has at present various assets which help generate significant advantages. The people of Sherbrooke only have to take the opportunities. However important the strategy is, it remains that the determination and confidence of the business community to attain the economic future which is within the reach of their ambitions and their opportunities are also essential.
I shall simply add that I intend to devote all my energy to the development of the area. I urge all parties concerned to support the efforts of all those men and women who strive to improve the current economic situation. On the federal government level, I intend to make use of all available opportunities and openings to help our region, so that we may, to the extent of our ability, efforts and possibilities, bring to Sherbrooke the continuing economic development it has been seeking for such a long time.
On June 19 last, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) announced the new textile and clothing policy for Canada. The ministers indicated that the government of Canada had started negotiations aimed at extending the restrictive agreements with our suppliers. This textile policy for Canada, I must point out, was favourably received at the time by both industry and workers. Six months after this new policy was announced, we can say that all in all, it has helped the industry significantly, but that some areas, especially the glove industry, have been affected, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce will have to look into this particular problem. Generally speaking, we can say that the textile industry now is one segment of our economy that is doing fairly well. I should like however, to return to that announcement made last June which reads in part as follows:
The government intends to propose a readjustment program designed to ensure that the Canadian textile and clothing industry is viable and competitive
and to revitalize the economy of communities that are most vulnerable to foreign competition.
The minister announced, and I quote:
A new program for which more than $250 million has been earmarked by the government over the next five years will be set up for the following purposes:
1-	To create new jobs in the communities affected by industrial readjustment;
2-	To make it possible for displaced workers to benefit from new job opportunities; and
3-	To promote the modernization of viable businesses in the textile and clothing industry.
These $250 million-if I understood well the announcement made last June-will be spent essentially in Canadian communities with textile and clothing plants, therefore mostly in Quebec. Approximately a month ago, more specifically on October 26 last, the Prime Minister announced the creation of the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, the terms of reference of which included, and 1 quote:
To promote the restructuration, regrouping and modernization of our textile and clothing industries, renew the economic basis of communities which depend largely on these industries and are therefore more likely to be adversely affected by the increasingly freer trade of these products, and to help the workers affected by these changes.
Mr. Speaker, this announcement is of tremendous importance for Sherbrooke and the Eastern Townships. In spite of efforts made by the governments in the past few years to help diversify our industrial structure to a greater extent, we have not yet succeeded in the Eastern Townships in giving impetus to the industrial restructuring process, which is of the utmost importance for the future of our region. Recent statistics indicate that the Eastern Townships area is one of the least advanced in Quebec with respect to its industrial structure. The communique states that the creation of the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board will work in close co-operation with the federal departments under the guidance of a special committee of ministers chaired by the Prime Minister so as to make sure that the industrial renewal, inasmuch as it affects the economy of the regions, the community groups and the labour force, does indeed meet the social and economic needs involved.
One of the basic characteristics of this new strategy is the pooling of efforts from the private and public sectors with a view to increasing competition in the designated sectors, diversifying the economic base of the communities involved and ensuring that the workers will benefit from new job opportunities. Finally, it is stated in the communique that in the coming months it will submit to the special committee of ministers recommendations concerning the communities which should be the first to benefit from the special assistance program. The board will also remain in close contact with the provincial authorities as well as labour leaders, employers and the communities involved. Mr. Speaker, I want to say right now that at the earliest opportunity I intend to get in touch with the
December 7, 1981

chairman of the board, in co-operation with local organizations. We want to make sure that the Eastern Townships and the Sherbrooke area will draw maximum benefits from the funds made available to the board. We intend to meet the members of that organization as soon as possible and, along with local organizations, I will not miss an opportunity of making recommendations to that committee. Mr. Speaker, a significant event took place in Sherbrooke last October. For the first time a subcommittee of the Canadian Parliament unanimously adopted a reference of the House of Commons to undertake a survey in Quebec within the DREE hearings to study on site the economic situation of those two regions, namely the Eastern Townships and the Gaspe peninsula. This first experiment in Quebec and the third in Canada has turned out to be a real success.
We cannot, for the time being, foretell what will happen, as the report will be tabled only in a few weeks' time, on the recommendations of the subcommittee which visited those two areas in Quebec. But we can, right now, state that all those who presented a paper before the members of the subcommittee unanimously expressed their satisfaction at the fact that a committee from the House of Commons had come to study and discuss economic problems at the grass root level. The reports which were presented in perce and Sherbrooke have shown that there was a widespread desire to see the Department of Regional Economic Expansion getting more deeply involved in the development of those areas whose economic growth is slow. While DREE's contribution to the economic development in Quebec was readily acknowledged, the desire was expressed that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which is supposed to help the deprived areas, enlarge its terms of reference and be provided with financial means and additional powers so that it may provide faster, more direct and more efficient aid. 1 can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that those field trips last fall have demonstrated to us the importance of providing the representatives of the people with the opportunity to see in situ the impact of some of their policies. We were able to detect a few shortcomings in DREE's policies, but also some of its benefits. Now we have to improve the procedures, as many speakers have suggested, so that this department may become the real co-ordinator of federal interventions and help the economic situation of the less advanced areas in Canada.
I sincerely hope that the new legislation governing the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which the minister says is supposed to be tabled early in 1982, will fulfil the wishes of the groups we met over the last two years, who would like DREE to redirect its economic action at the regional level. When the law is tabled I shall elaborate on that a little further but for the time being, Mr. Speaker, I only want to point out that DREE has proved a big help in the economic field in many regions of Canada, and must redirect its course so as to
The Budget-Mr. Pelletier
play a more efficient part as the foremost dynamic force in areas of slow economic growth.
Mr. Speaker, statistics recently published about the unemployment rate fail, in my humble opinion, to express the seriousness of the situation in my area. We are a town, and have often been described as such, of institutions. I sincerely hope that we will examine the plight of this area as soon as possible. The unemployment problem among young people is a responsibility of all levels of governments and of private industry as well. We should work together to suggest means to resolve this problem and help young workers.
Even though I have pointed out, on many occasions but especially over the last few years, the stunning number of jobless young people in our area, I ought to add that there are many mature workers who are out of work as well and I feel we should make a special effort to help them make a decent living. Unemployment is a social scourge that government should and must endeavour to eliminate, by working in cooperation with all persons concerned. No one can look with equanimity at the waste of talent and intelligence caused by this unused potential. If the government does not respond to my cries of alarm, at least it should not be insensitive to the distress of the many unemployed workers.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that a good way to co-ordinate the economic policies that I mentioned earlier, would be to hold an economic conference on the area in question. At the first stage, we could hold a meeting in Sherbrooke, and at the second stage extend it to the whole region and in this manner we could exercise a greater pressure on the different levels of governments.
Let us first agree on the priorities, the directions at the Sherbrooke level, let us examine the specifics of action. When this is done, we can invite the greater area of the Eastern Townships to join us in a common development effort, because the economic development of the Sherbrooke area is very closely linked to that of the Eastern Townships, and vice versa. That economic summit, in addition to enabling us to see what the situation is and determine the directions to follow, will also enable us to establish the major priorities for the area over the next few years. I submit that this is essential. In the last few years, we had economic summits in our area on the textile, footwear and furniture industries, therefore an economic summit would enable us to know the state of all industries in Sherbrooke and give us the opportunity to decide on the direction we want to follow for our area.

MCDONALD ROYAL COMMISSION-QUERY RESPECTING REPORT ABRIDGEMENTS.-(B) PREPARATION OF INDEX TO REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 25, at page 13240 in Hansard, I put two questions to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) relating to the documents and the report of the McDonald Commission. The first of these was to seek his assurance that those deletions, which we all understand were made in the report, are in safekeeping and will be made available to the public in due course; second, that because of the complexity and the volume of the report, some effort be made to prepare an index to the three documents. What I therefore seek is an assurance that the abridgements will be preserved and made available to the public in due course; second, we would like an index.
My worries are of three kinds. The first concerns these deletions. I quite understand the qualms of the commissioners when they say that they feel it is desirable and in the public interest to withhold some of the report, particularly if there is a risk of imperilling the security of Canada. They also consider that the identity of individuals and organizations should be safeguarded, particularly as they might be liable to prosecution in the course of time. In the report, they did not wish to prejudice the process. That is quite understandable.
What I find to be a little lacking in assurance, giving me cause to worry, is that this particular government, which has a record of having lost or mislaid or deliberately allowing certain
documents to be destroyed which now ought to be in the public domain, might cause these particular chapters of the McDonald commission report to disappear as well.
I think, for example, of the loss of the Mackenzie King diary, one of the important Mackenzie King diaries related to the Gouzenko papers. That document has disappeared. 1 quite recognize that it did not disappear at the archives. However, somehow or other, it was not properly safeguarded until the executors had a chance to look at it, and it has now disappeared. I am sure it is a valuable document because it specifically dealt with the Gouzenko matter.
The second problem involving my mistrust of the government in these matters arises from the fact that after the usual 30 years of preventing the public scrutiny of documents related to the Taschereau-Kellogg report on the Gouzenko matter, we learned that an extra ten years would be added for reasons which were never clear. Subsequently we learned that another solicitor general of another government tried to get access to those documents to see whether they ought to be made public, but he was denied access to them.
The next stage in that particular operation was that the Liberal government was returned to office and ordered, under some pressure I should add, those documents to be re-examined to see whether they could be released. Now they are released. But we have no certainty that in the interim some of them have not disappeared. I do not want the McDonald commission documents to disappear.
The third misgiving I have is the mystery surrounding the Featherbed files and where they went. Nobody seems to be able to say where they went. If they can disappear, what about documents relating to the McDonald commission?
Fourth, there was the deliberate destruction of the Checkmate files, which is reported upon in the McDonald report. Those four reasons give me ample cause to have misgivings about the lost documents.
All these matters, together with the refusal of cabinet to accept final responsibility for RCMP actions, as mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) give me concern. In a 1977 press conference, the Prime Minister stated:
It is a matter of stating as a principle that the particular minister of the day should not have a right to know what the police are doing constantly in their investigative practices, what they are looking at, and what they are looking for, and the way in which they are doing it.
That, I suggest, is not a proper expression of ministerial responsibility and gives me concern about the possible loss of these documents.
On those grounds, I think I am amply justified in seeking the assurance of the government that these documents are in safekeeping and that they will, in due course, be made available to the public.
The other matter of the index arises mainly from the complexity of this report. It is a long report and contains thousands of pages. It is not easy to follow one's way through
December 7, 1981

it. An index would be most helpful. I would appreciate getting from the government some sort of an assurance that the index that has been prepared by the commission itself, which I believe was put on a computer tape, will be available in due course. I hope not too far down the road that it will be available to the general public so that we will all be able to find our way through this very complicated report. I do hope I will get those two assurances, although I doubt it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does the hon. member want the response? I shall give it in my fashion, not his. If he has a little patience, he may learn something.
There was the assurance that nothing was deleted which reported conduct of any individual which was criticized by the commission.
In addition, with regard to the third report, there has been agreement with the commission to delay publication of those chapters of Part IV of the report that recommend referrals of particular matters to the attorneys general and to the commissioner for possible disciplinary action. These chapters, together with related material identified by the commissioners, have been conveyed to the attorneys general for their consideration.
The hon. member has asked where the deletions have been made, but the House will understand that that sort of informa-
Adjournment Debate
tion cannot be disclosed lest that disclosure would reveal clues to the precise matters which have been expurgated. It is not, therefore, possible to go beyond stating the grounds on which the deletions were made. As for the report as presented to the governor in council, it has been filed with the Privy Council office where it is under the control and in the care of the custodian of the documents and records of the commission, the Clerk of the Privy Council and secretary to the cabinet.
With regard to the editing done to the report, it should be recalled that the government made as few deletions as was consistent with our security needs, that those made had the full support of the commissioners, and that the publication of the report constitutes an unprecedented public disclosure of our security affairs.
The second matter raised by the hon. member in his questions was access to an index to the report. Upon inquiry, I have ascertained that no computer records or index of the report was made by the commission. I can also inform the House that the government is not considering the preparation of an index to these volumes.
The report is the result of the extensive work conducted by the commission, not the government. I would remind the hon. member that this report has been publicly available for more than three months, giving ample time for him to have read it. It should be noted that the report contains a detailed and lengthy table of contents and has been cross-referenced. For this reason, the government sees no reason to go to the expense of preparing the index that has been proposed by the hon. member.

AGRICULTURE-ESTABLISHMENT OF WESTERN GRAINS RESEARCH FOUNDATION -(B) AVAILABILITY OF FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 21 last I posed a question, as recorded at page 12023 of Hansard, to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to determine whether or not he supported the presentation of a group of western farm organizations which set up the Western Grains Research Foundation. Their presentation requested that the $9 million presently in the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund be paid to their foundation and that a voluntary levy of one tenth of 1 per cent on grain sales also be part of their funding.
The minister indicated he had not met with the foundation, but they had met with his officials and he had not, at the time I asked the question, had an opportunity to see the report from his officials.
In response to my supplementary question, recorded again at page 12023 of Hansard, he seemed to try to cast a doubt on the fact that the $9 million in the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund in fact belonged to the producers. He said, "He knows that that money belongs to both the government-", and after interruption he continued by saying, "-was contributed to by the producers". If one refers back to the debate on February 3, 1981, at page 6845, one will see that the minister referred to the fund in the following terms:

December 7, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Having this money work for prairie farmers through research is the ideal situation because, after all, it is the farmers' money.
The debate in question on that date was on second reading of a private member's bill, Bill C-245, proposed by myself, to repeal the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and to set up a trust consisting of four trustees, three of whom would be producers listed in permit books as actual producers, one from each of the three prairie provinces, and as the fourth a man expert in the field of research and development in cereal and oilseeds, who would be the chairman of the trust. The trustees would hold the $9 million presently in the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund in trust and use the interest earned on the money for research and development in cereal and oil seeds suitable for production in the Canadian Wheat Board area.
I raised the point in the debate that some $9,066,972 has been standing to the credit of the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund since 1972 and that the government has been using that money without payment of interest since that time. It is farmers' money; and if interest had been paid since the inception of the fund, the fund itself would have doubled or tripled in size by this time. At rates that have prevailed for the past year, the fund would have been earning between $3,500 and $4,000 per day. As each day goes by, this interest is lost to research in the Canadian Wheat Board area.
The minister was not prepared to approve my bill in February of 1981, arguing that his department was in the process of putting the final touches to his own bill which he would be presenting to Parliament. Almost a year has gone by, Mr. Speaker, and his bill has not yet seen the light of day.
He did agree during the debate on February, 1981, to send the subject matter of my bill to committee for a study, but such a study has never taken place. In the meantime, the Grains Research Foundation has been set up by a group of western farm organizations-I should say the group of western farm organizations, including all the western farm organizations with one exception-and the aims and objects of the trust that they propose to set up is the same as the aims and objects which I set forth in my Bill C-245. I have indicated to the foundation that they have my complete and full support.
I believe it is incumbent upon the Minister of Agriculture to indicate his reaction to the Western Grains Research Foundation proposal, and whether or not he is prepared to introduce legislation transferring the $9 million to that foundation. I caution him that every day of delay on his part means between $3,500 and $4,000 lost to western grain research, and it is he who must assume full responsibility and answer to the western grain producers.
I know his answer has been that the money is in a non-interest bearing fund, but I think it is an absolute disgrace that producers' money has sat in an account since 1972, been used by the government and has not drawn one cent of interest.
If the minister is indicating that he plans on bringing in a bill of his own, I would suggest that he do so without further delay. I would like to tell him quite frankly, however, that if
his bill is such that he or his department retains control of the fund and it does not provide for control of the fund by the producers of western Canada, he will certainly not gain the approval of members on this side of the House.
In closing, I want to make it quite clear that it was not my intention, and it is not the intention of the Western Grains Research Foundation when they submitted their proposal, to downgrade or detract from the great work that the research branch of the Department of Agriculture has carried out. They are doing excellent work, but they are limited in their funds and they are doing research in areas that would not ordinarily be the priority of producers who had their own ideas on what should be done. This foundation would not detract from the department, but would give the producer an opportunity to decide what particular type of research he wants. There is a shortage of researchers, I would like to point out. In talking to the research foundation members, I found out that perhaps it might be part of their plan to fund some senior students who would like to further their education in order to become researchers. I understand that university students from Canada who are taking their degree do not wish to further their education because it is not worth it. It is only people from abroad who take their Master's degree or do their doctorate in research.
It is my hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ostiguy) in responding to my remarks tonight will at least give us some indication of what the minister plans to do with respect to the $9 million, and I would hope that he appreciates the fact that there is a great deal of urgency because of the interest lost on this money on a daily basis.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention the timeliness of the hon. member's question considering that the Conference on Agricultural Outlooks for the Eighties opened this morning. As the hon. member most appropriately remarked, it was precisely on October 21, 1981, the very day that he asked the Minister a question on this issue, that the Federation of Agriculture and the Western Grain foundation submitted to the officials of the Department of Agriculture a proposal providing for a transfer of funds, the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund in order to promote research.
Since then the Minister has been and continues to be in close contact with the President of the Treasury Board, and this very day he was meeting with the representatives of both organizations, that is Mr. Hamilton of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and Mr. Strath of the Western Grain Research Foundation, to consider whatever changes Agriculture Canada or the Treasury Board might have to make in
December 7, 1981

order to make this $9 million fund provide better support for research.
The hon. member is no doubt aware that agricultural research is dealt with directly in the document tabled by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) entitled "The Agri-food Strategy for the Eighties". Agriculture Canada does realize that research is a must and we agree with the hon. member that part of those funds could be transferred to the producers. We hope that following the meeting the Minister is having today and tomorrow with the spokesmen for both organizations, he will be able to give us an answer before the end of the year. I do not have a definite answer at this moment. However during these meetings table hold in the next two or three days here in Ottawa as I just said, with the representatives of both organizations, and as we know the federal-provincial conference of ministers of agriculture will also be held here on Wednesday-the minister will have ample opportunity to discuss this issue with all parties concerned. Let us not forget that Agriculture Canada has invested over $200 million in agricultural research. We are all aware of the fact that Canadian agriculture must develop and improve its productivity, as the various speakers were saying this morning in presenting their papers at the meeting of the federal conference on agriculture for the eighties, and also that its development is directly related to that of research.

AGRICULTURE-REFINANCING OF CO-OPERATIVE IMPLEMENTS OF WINNIPEG.-(B) AMOUNT OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention tonight is with regard to a problem of Co-op Implements of Winnipeg, a farm co-operative which has been producing implements in the west for a number of years. Since its organization in Canada in 1958, Co-op Implements have made dramatic progress. Gross sales for the fiscal year ending October 31 this year have increased 84 per cent, from $57 million in 1978 to $105 million in 1981. The work force of Co-op Implements has increased 27 per cent in this timeframe, from 773 in October 1978 to 982 on October 31, 1981. Expenditures on research and development by Co-op Implements have increased 464 per cent in that period, from $285,000 in 1978 to $1.6 million in 1981, 1.5 per cent of its sales, which is a very good record for any industry. Co-op Implements have turned around from $3.8 million loss in 1978 to $1.6 million profit in 1979. Despite the soaring interest costs, heavy investments in research and development and a million dollar employee training program in 1980, losses were kept below $1 million. The final results for 1981 are not yet available, but it would seem they will break even. Except for one factor, this year they would have made a profit.
The interest bill of Co-op Implements for 1981 was $105 million. They have an interest bill of approximately $35,000 a
Adjournment Debate
day. It is another case of interest rates affecting the viability of an industry.
The key line of this report on Co-op Implements is probably this last line which says that profits would have been assured in 1981 had the supposed equity package been in place. Mr. Speaker, my intervention is exactly on that basis.
The proposed package was a $35.5 million package. Nine and a half million dollars was to be raised by the organizations in the co-ops in western Canada. Five million dollars was to be raised by the membership of Co-Op Implements, by farmers such as myself. Seven million dollars was to be raised by the provinces. The fourth group to contribute to this package was $14 million by the federal government.
On December 4, 1981, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made the following statement in a press release: Financial Aid to Co-op Implements
-Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan today announced that cabinet has proposed a total of $14 million in federal funding to assist Co-operative Implements of Winnipeg.
That was a very misleading statement. If one were to turn to the second last paragraph of the same press release, one would find that it states that:
The outstanding portion of this contribution, about $7.5 million, will be forgiven as part of the total assistance to the company.
The request was for $14 million. The suggestion by the federal government is for $6.5 million. The $7.5 million majority of the federal contribution is a loan, a write-off. The governments of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta have asked for a $14 million contribution in cash from the federal government. This is somewhat similar to the contribution which was asked for previously by the Government of Ontario when Chrysler Canada Ltd. was in trouble.
The proposal of the Minister of Agriculture is not new to the governments of the prairies, and it was not acceptable when it was known. It will not become acceptable because it has been made public.
Let us look at some comparisons. During the last couple of weeks, $6.5 million in grants was given to a hotel complex in Windsor which will be operated by the Hilton Corporation. Thirty million dollars in grants was given to what we called in the west the Deutz company, which produces diesel tractors in the east. This $30 million was contributed to these companies so as to give them a basis for operation; but instead, a company in the west, which is Canadian owned and Canadian operated with 1,000 employees, was offered a paltry $6.5 million, compared to the $14 million that it requested. I want to know from the minister or his parliamentary secretary right now exactly what we can expect from the federal government in this situation. How much can we expect, and when can we expect it?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for

December 7, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) concerning Co-operative Implements of Winnipeg, I must say that the figures he has quoted are almost accurate, except that he stated that the government contributed to Massey-Ferguson, to Chrysler and to White Implement. I would like to remind the hon. member that these companies received a loan guarantee while Co-operative Implements of Winnipeg received grants on various occasions, of which the first was an interest-free grant of $7 million, I believe, which, with $3 million in interest, would represent, according to my calculation about S10 million in direct assistance.
We recognize the magnificent contribution of this company in western Canada. It manufactures fine equipment, but we still have to look at its operations, and this is why it will perhaps be impossible to go any further this evening, as the minister and the department are now considering, along with the provinces, the various means available to save or to assist
financially Co-operative Implements of Winnipeg. The hon. member himself mentioned the high interest rates, but it still remains that various farm machinery manufacturers are going through a rather difficult period. Of course, the American and European markets are not as sound as they were. Equipment costs, wages, and everything else have increased in the last few years, and it seems that farmers are thinking twice about investing heavily in farm machinery. As I said earlier, I am sorry that I am not able to provide more information, but we are aware of the situation described by the hon. member for Prince Albert.
